Its signature habit is packing 3-6 enumerated facts into a single sentence as "(1)…(2)…(3)…" — six answers do this. Every other file in the zone interrupts theory with a diagram or code block every 2-3 paragraphs; this one runs 68 paragraphs without a break, in the file a candidate is most likely to read end-to-end on a phone.
- Untranslated H1s in 7 of 9 RU files have broken the RU locale's internal navigation. The RU glossary points at articles by Russian names (Основы CI/CD, Основы Docker, Стратегии деплоя, Окружения и конфигурация, Мониторинг и наблюдаемость) that match no heading, while ru/01's own 'what's next' block points at the same articles by their English names. Two incompatible naming systems inside one locale, neither of which resolves.

**Прочее:** Zone question — no, the glossary does not excuse the other eight files, and it could not even if it were linked: it omits VM, PR, MR, TLS, CDN, SDK, IAM, JWT, S3, EC2, OS, UID, SHA, SaaS, CLI, UI, which the other files use unexpanded. No file links to it at an acronym's first use; only 01 mentions it once in a 'what's next' block. The glossary itself reads well as reference prose (C=5: every entry leads with its definition) but is a 107-paragraph wall with 51-62 over-long paragraphs and zero diagrams or tables, and has 4 dangling cross-references — *Span*, *Sidecar*, *Exec form* and *Monitoring* are pointed at but have no entries in either locale.
Outside my remit but it blocks comprehension: en/07 L568 and ru/07 L570 say a *readiness* probe checking external dependencies causes pod restarts; the anti-pattern section 150 lines earlier correctly says *liveness*, and 09 words the same trap correctly. A reader who noticed the first version will not trust either.
Small mechanical defects: ru/07 «SLI пропускной сп.:количество» (missing space), ru/02 «упакованных в одну вызов», ru/08 «CloudFormation создаёт ими управляет» (missing «и»). en/08's cross-reference *[Environments and Config]* does not match that article's H1 'Environments and Configuration'.
The verdict is systemic-refactor rather than targeted-fixes because two of seven criteria (A 2.9, G 2.7) fail across all 18 / all 9 RU files with one shared root cause each — not because the depth or structure is wrong. B/C/D/E are genuinely strong (3.5-4.6); the ASCII diagrams and the definition-first section openings are the best thing in this zone and should be left alone.

### css-html (статьи) — точечные правки

- The Russian version is the harder one, not the easier one — reversing the usual assumption. RU wins on syntax (B 4.4 vs 3.9, because Russian sentences here are genuinely shorter) but loses on terminology (A 2.8 vs 3.0, G 3.0) because the translation pass systematically drops the clarifying material the English carries: TTI's gloss (ru/09:265 vs en/09:265), CLS's gloss (ru/07:444 vs en/07:446), the written-out "assistive technologies" that makes AT guessable (ru/11:209 vs en/11:209), the clamp() formula line (ru/07:297), the IE/Edge caveat on focusable="false" (ru/01:154), the YAML remark (ru/09:390), and — worst — the entire six-example "Common accessibility mistakes" section of the site's only a11y article (ru/01, 15 headings vs 22, 24 fences vs 36). Any fix pass must diff ru against en per file, not read each locale on its own.
- Russian articles code-switch where they should translate, in two distinct forms. (a) Multi-word English spec terms are left in Latin script mid-sentence — "Также создаёт: stacking context, block formatting context, containing block" (ru/08:233, repeated 239, 382; ru/11:229) — even though this same site translates all three elsewhere ("контекст наложения" ru/05, "контекст блочного форматирования" ru/02). (b) English words get Russian morphology bolted on to make non-words: "непромоутированных" (ru/11:163), "авторинг" (ru/09:485,503), "интринсическое/интринсическая/интринсический" (ru/07:433,435; ru/04:244; ru/11:39), "флюидный" (ru/07:261,291), "bucket-ы" (ru/06:447; ru/11:111), "drawer-ы" (ru/08:200; ru/11:25), "стилизованные" for "layered" (ru/06:210,453; ru/11:111 — this one destroys the sentence's meaning). Rule for the style guide: if the term has an established Russian form, use it and put the English in parentheses once; never inflect an English stem.
- Abbreviations are introduced by a file the reader may not have opened, or by a section that comes later in the same file. BFC is used in en/02:118 and ru/02:118 but only defined at line 146 of the same file; in file 11 BFC's first use (line 13) is one question before its definition (line 17). ARIA is expanded only in 01, yet used 5x in 11. GPU (22x in 08, 7x in 11), CSSOM, CPU, DOM and VRAM are treated as shared vocabulary across 08 and 11. Because these files are read out of order and 11 is the natural entry point for interview prep, 11 is the file where the abbreviation debt lands hardest (A=1 in both locales).
- File 11 inverts the zone's own best habit. The zone's outstanding strength is the answer-first lead — C scores 5 in all 22 files, and 11 is the purest example ("346px." / "No — one fraction of the available free space" / "Only transform and opacity."). But 11 pairs that with the zone's worst structure: 3,769 EN / 3,073 RU words, 33 over-long paragraphs, 36 EN sentences over 25 words, and zero code fences, tables or diagrams in either locale — in a file whose every answer is about code. The other ten articles average one code fence per ~85 words. The fix is not to cut answers but to let each answer show the two lines of CSS it is describing.
- Two authoring self-corrections survived into published English prose, both in en/05 (line 128 "... wait, actually ..." and the Fix 2 block at 309-317 that retracts its own fix). Both are absent from ru/05, which means the Russian pass caught what the English pass did not — so English files need the same second read the Russian ones evidently got. Related smaller slips of the same kind: en/02:219 has a stray `**` closing a bold heading, en/03:227 says "use `margin-auto`" for `margin: auto`, en/06:74 and en/09:74 both read "Overriding is trivially:", ru/03:3 has "два оси" for "две оси", ru/11:215 has "объходить" for "обходить", and en/04:386 vs ru/04:386 disagree on `data-weekday="1"` vs `"2"` under an identical "Tuesday" comment.

**Прочее:** Zone-specific verdict on 01, the site's only real a11y article: a reader with no ARIA/WCAG/screen-reader vocabulary CAN follow the EN version, with four stumbles — "screen reader" and "announce" are used from line 19 as if known, "landmarks" arrives undefined at line 37, WCAG appears once at line 326 never expanded, and "input modality" carries the whole :focus-visible answer at line 454 while being the most opaque phrase in the file. Everything else is well built: ARIA is expanded on first use, the accessibility tree is explained before it is used, and the div-vs-button table is the best scaffolding in the zone. The RU version is materially worse for that reader: same four gaps plus "ориентиры" (a literal calque of landmarks with no currency in Russian a11y writing), bare "AT" (unguessable, since the RU expansion is "вспомогательные технологии"), "disclosure-виджетов" and "модальность ввода" — and it is missing the six-mistake practical section entirely. Recommended minimum: a four-line glossary paragraph after the H1 (screen reader, accessibility tree, landmark, WCAG) in both locales, plus restoring the missing RU section. Mechanical density (11.8 flags/1k) does understate this zone's problems only in files 05, 08 and 11; files 02, 03, 04 and 10 are genuinely ship-ready and 03 is the best-written article in the zone in both locales.

### css-html-practice (вопросы+quiz) — системный рефактор

- The quiz answer key is broken at scale, and the explanations are where it shows. 13 of 30 items have an `explanation` that contradicts its own `correctIndex`, miscounts, or answers a different question than the one asked: quiz-2, 5, 8, 11, 12, 15, 17, 21, 22, 26, 27, 29 plus quiz-1's mis-stated (1,3,1). Two of them (quiz-2, quiz-8) contain unedited model self-talk — 'Wait, let me recalculate', 'I apologize—let me verify' — and quiz-26 has no correct option among its four. Because rubric C is scored on the explanation, this alone puts the quiz at C=1: a reader who trusts the explanation is actively taught the wrong answer. Layered on top, the key is guessable without reading: `correctIndex` is 0 in 21 of 30 items (70%; 3 each for 1, 2 and 3), and in 14 of those the index-0 option is also the longest — 'pick the first, longest option' scores about 70%.
- The bank is strong on C and weak on E in the same specific way: it always tells you the rule and rarely shows you the result. Only 13 of 48 answers put a rendered outcome inside a code comment (`/* rendered width: 200 + 20*2 + 2*2 = 244px */` in q-1, `auto-fill -> 3 items stay 200px wide` in q-21, `/* desugars to: .card:hover */` in q-38); the other 35 use comments that label *intent* ('horizontal centering', 'creates a positioning context') and leave the visual outcome to be imagined. The habit thins out as difficulty rises — 6/20 junior answers state an outcome, 1/8 advanced ones — so the questions that most need a picture (q-31 stacking order, q-39 subgrid footer alignment, q-35 container queries, q-40 the transition pseudo-element tree) have none. There is not a single box-drawing diagram in all 48 answers, even though articles 02, 03 and 04 use them for the very same box model, flexbox and auto-fit topics.
- One contiguous block of the bank was authored from a mislabelled template: every code fence in css-html-q-21 through q-30 is tagged ```typescript, in both locales. 18 of those 19 blocks contain plain CSS or HTML, so the reader gets CSS coloured as TypeScript on a phone. It is a mechanical, zero-risk fix confined to ten entries, and the correct labels (```css, ```html, ```javascript) are already used correctly everywhere else in the file.

**Прочее:** RU/EN asymmetry runs opposite to the articles. In the question bank RU is complete (0.92 of EN word count, nothing dropped) and is the *easier* locale: 31.9% long sentences vs 44.4% EN, no 70-word sentences, and almost no calques. EN is harder — idioms a B1-B2 reader will stall on ('belt-and-suspenders', 'trips people up', 'eat into', 'warm up a connection'), plus four EN-only unexpanded acronyms (CJK, FLIP, VRAM, CPU). The bank RU's own weakness is untranslated English nouns inflected into Russian: «скроллящемуся предку», «неслоёные/слоёные стили», «стилшитах», «тем-зависимых», «лейаута», and «вьюпорт» vs «viewport» used inconsistently across entries. The quiz reverses this: RU is the weaker locale there (G=2) — it drops clarifying words (quiz-19 'screen reader context' -> «контекста экрана», quiz-27 loses the entire flex derivation), and translates one CSS box four different ways. Its one advantage is accidental: the self-talk in quiz-2 and quiz-8 was cleaned out of RU while the wrong `correctIndex` was left in both. Verdict is systemic-refactor because of the quiz alone; the 48-question bank on its own would be targeted-fixes (C=5, answer-first throughout, same strength the articles showed).

### ddd (вопросы) — точечные правки

- This is the best-written bank of the two zones I audited and the fixes are genuinely local — but it inherits one habit from the whole site: the load-bearing practical sentence of an entry is always the longest one in it. ddd-q-9's five-way pattern mapping is 96 words, ddd-q-8's 'how to actually enforce a rich model' is 71 words, ddd-q-12's Common pitfall is 53. The definitional sentences are short and clear; the sentence a reader would act on is the one they cannot parse. 49.4% of en sentences exceed 25 words against 30.1% ru, so this hits the English reader roughly 1.6x as hard. Nearly every one of these long sentences is a list wearing prose clothing — splitting at the semicolons into a bullet list preserves every claim and costs nothing.
- The Russian is markedly better than the English here, and much better than the Russian in the solid-grasp bank. It reads as written rather than translated («издержки, которые реально бьют по команде», «размазан по обработчикам», «списание прошло, а резервирование склада упало»). The only recurring G defect is mixed-language headings, where the connective words rather than the DDD terms are left in English — «Trade-offs DDD — глубже очевидного», «Anemic vs Rich Domain Model», «Entity vs Value Object». The term names should stay untranslated; the `vs` and the `Trade-offs` should not.
- Code samples drift out of sync with each other because entries are written standalone but share a running domain (Order / Money / OrderRepository). `Money.zero()` in q-3 and q-8 contradicts the invariant q-10 explicitly stops to teach (`Money.zero("USD")`); `findById` is nullable in q-4 and treated as non-null in q-6; `OrderSummaryProjector` (q-12) and `Order` (q-5) reference `this.` fields that no constructor declares, breaking a `constructor(private ...)` convention every other class in the file follows. Since the reader meets these entries in arbitrary order, each snippet has to hold the shared contract on its own.
- Only one entry in fifteen warms up before answering — but it is a consistent tell of the 'senior' framing. ddd-q-10 opens 'At senior level, the interesting part isn't just "what's an aggregate"...', ddd-q-13 opens by relaying a trade-off in order to call it shallow, ddd-q-14's heading is 'the Sharp Edges'. Elsewhere the leads are exemplary pyramid — ddd-q-1's 'The split comes down to how you compare two objects and whether you need to track one of them over time' answers before it defines anything. The fix is to delete the meta-clause and promote sentence two.

**Прочее:** The ddd bank has no articles and, unlike solid-grasp, no theory anywhere else on the site either — grep finds no ddd topic or course. That makes the cold `DDD` in q-3/q-5/q-6/q-11..q-15 and the bare `ACL` in q-9/q-13 unrecoverable for the reader: there is nothing to click through to. If article coverage is not planned, first-use expansion inside each entry is not a nicety here, it is the only mechanism available. Content quality itself is high and needs no depth changes: the 15 questions are well-sequenced (6 middle / 6 senior / 3 advanced), internally consistent on doctrine, and go past the usual tutorial level on Event Sourcing versioning/snapshotting/replay determinism (q-14) and saga idempotency (q-15).

### docker (вопросы+quiz) — системный рефактор

- The question bank has one dominant shape and it is almost right: a strong plain-language lead sentence (indirect_leads is 0.0% in both locales — rubric C is the zone's best score at 4), then a single dense paragraph that packs every remaining fact into 55-118-word semicolon chains, then the code example. The fix is mechanical and repeats in 14 of 20 answers: split the one paragraph into labelled short items, and move the existing code block ABOVE the prose that describes it. Nothing technical needs to change — docker-q-5, -9, -12, -14, -17, -20 are all the same edit.
- The quiz layer is not a language problem, it is an unedited generated artefact. Five signals, all mechanical and all invisible to a prose-level flag script: (1) zero ``` fences in the entire file, so all five code snippets render as stray language tags plus unformatted text; (2) ids jump 1-5, 7, 9-10, 12-15 — three items were deleted from a generated set of 15 and nothing was renumbered or re-balanced; (3) two snippets are decoration that contradicts their own answer (quiz-14's `VOLUME` declares the anonymous volume the answer warns against) or cannot build (quiz-12); (4) three stems glue two or three questions together and only the last one matches the options; (5) 12 items cover just 6 concepts — CMD-vs-ENTRYPOINT three times (quiz-2, -10, -13), volumes three times (quiz-5, -9, -14), multi-stage twice (quiz-4, -12) — while 14 of the bank's 20 topics (limits, health checks, non-root USER, BuildKit cache, .dockerignore, signals, socket) are never assessed at all.
- The docker page teaches Linux-kernel vocabulary it never defines, because the file that does define it lives in another topic. namespaces, cgroups, PID 1, OOM killer, hypervisor and UID all appear bare in the question bank; cicd-devops/04-docker-essentials.md expands namespaces and cgroups in prose AND draws the VM-vs-container box diagram — and the reader on the Docker page never sees it. Since the bank is the only Docker theory on that page, every one of these needs a first-use gloss inside the bank itself.
- RU and EN diverge in difficulty in opposite directions for the two content types. In the bank, EN is the harder version (3798 words vs 3379, 66 long sentences vs 49 — 48.2% vs 35.3%), the usual ~19% English inflation pushing borderline sentences over the limit. In the quiz it flips: RU is the weaker text, not because of length but because the terminology is machine-generated («привязанные монты», «тома оверлея», «наложенных сетей», «для производства») and inconsistent with the RU question bank sitting right next to it, which uses the normal industry terms.

**Прочее:** Quiz numbers, computed exactly. (a) The correct option is the longest option in 9/12 items in BOTH locales (75%); mean correct-option length 112.6 chars vs 75.2 for distractors in EN (1.50x), 132.0 vs 80.3 in RU (1.64x) — a reader who just picks the longest option scores 75% without knowing Docker. (b) correctIndex: 0 -> 8 items (67%), 1 -> 3, 2 -> 1, 3 -> 0 (never). Less extreme than quiz/security (25/25 at index 0) or quiz/git (20/20), but index 3 is dead and index 0 is still two thirds; the topic-quiz route renders options in file order, so it is visible. (c) Contradictions: quiz-2's marked answer is factually wrong and is contradicted by quiz-10, quiz-13, its own explanation, and cicd-devops/04-docker-essentials.md line 218; quiz-14's snippet declares an anonymous volume while the answer says use named ones; quiz-15's option 0 reads as if the DEFAULT bridge network gives DNS discovery, which docker-q-8 flags as its 'common pitfall' (true under Compose only because Compose creates a user-defined bridge). Also note cicd-devops/04 line 266 lists FROM/RUN/COPY/ADD as the layer-creating instructions, then its own diagram at line 273 counts 'Layer 2: WORKDIR /app' — a reader who studied that article would answer quiz-7 differently. (d) Artifacts: zero ``` fences in the file (5 items affected); id gaps at 6, 8, 11; three multi-question stems; near-duplicate items (quiz-10 and quiz-13 are the same question). (e) Explanations referencing option positions: ZERO — clean, no 'the first option'/'вариант A' anywhere. The related defect is that 9 of 12 explanations reuse >=69% of the correct option's own words, so they restate rather than teach. Verdict is systemic-refactor on the strength of the quiz half; the question bank alone would be targeted-fixes (its structure is sound, it needs a sentence-splitting and abbreviation pass, not a rewrite).

### event-driven (вопросы) — системный рефактор

- Every senior/advanced entry packs an enumerated list of 3-4 independent ideas into ONE sentence using inline `(1)…(2)…(3)…` markers, producing 90-174-word sentences: q-12 (174w en / 158w ru), q-10 (121w), q-16 (120w), q-21 (117w), q-24 (91w). 73.8% of EN sentences and 62.6% of RU sentences are over the length threshold. The items are already separate thoughts — the same file uses real markdown bullets correctly in q-1 and q-15, so this is a habit, not a constraint.
- The single code example always sits at the very end, after all the theory, and in the hardest entries it illustrates the easiest part of the answer rather than the part that needed anchoring: q-15 gives three broker-comparison paragraphs then a snippet about seeking an offset; q-21 defines four compatibility modes and four breaking changes then shows only the safe additive case; q-12 lists four scaling challenges then shows snapshot loading, which was challenge (1). The dense middle of each answer has nothing to hold on to.
- Acronyms are spelled out in the one entry that happens to introduce them and used bare everywhere else — CQRS is expanded once, in q-5's question text, then used unexplained in q-9, q-10, q-12 and q-18; CRUD is never expanded in either locale. A question bank is read one card at a time in random order, so per-entry expansion is the only expansion that counts.
- The RU text is broadly living Russian, but breaks into transliteration exactly where the English term is a verb: «ключуйте» (key by), «истекайте записи» (expire entries), «переретраенное сообщение» (retried), «переразмеренный/недоразмеренный агрегат» (oversized/undersized), «просто в осмыслении» (simple to reason about). Nouns get borrowed cleanly; verbs get mangled.

**Прочее:** The bank has no theory article behind it: the closest material (nestjs/08-cqrs-pattern, architecture/05, system-design/05) is invisible from this page, so every acronym has to be carried by the entry itself — this raises the weight of criterion A above its usual level here. EN is measurably harder than RU (6896 vs 6190 words, 73.8% vs 62.6% long sentences), which is the reverse of what the ~19% expansion rule would predict as merely borderline; the EN register also leans idiomatic ("papers the wall", "poison message", "buys you nothing", "a tax you pay on every deploy"). Content depth is genuinely senior throughout and should not be touched — every finding above is language-level. One non-readability note: q-16's `streamHead` is declared and never used.

### git (вопросы+quiz) — системный рефактор

- The quiz bank reads as unverified generated output that was never opened after generation. Four independent signals, all measured over the full 20 items: `correctIndex` is 0 for all twenty; the correct option is the longest in 17/20 EN and 15/20 RU (mean 109 vs 80 chars EN, 118 vs 86 RU), so pick-the-longest scores 85% with zero Git knowledge; six items cite option positions («Вариант 1», "Options 2, 3, and 4") that `shuffleOptions` in src/lib/quiz-utils.ts destroys at render time; and two items give opposite answers to the same question (git-quiz-15 says detached-HEAD work is lost, git-quiz-19 says reflog recovers it). No literal "Wait, let me recalculate" artifacts were found here, but the option-position references are the same class of defect.
- Zone-specific (rubric E): Git answers are taught by describing history in prose and then listing the commands you would type, with the output cut off. Only 3 of 20 question-bank entries print anything Git would actually display (q-8's rebase todo list, q-9's conflict markers, q-16's one reflog line), and not a single entry in either file shows a before/after commit graph — including q-7 (rebase vs merge), q-4 and q-10 (branching models), and quiz items 1/11/16, whose entire subject is what the history looks like afterwards. The two ASCII attempts that do exist (quiz-11, quiz-16) are misaligned rows with no branch point.
- Russian quality is bimodal inside one zone. The question bank is hand-written, idiomatic Russian — «сплющивается внутрь develop», «кто и почему нарезал релиз», «шторм конфликтов» — and scores 4 on G. The quiz is literal machine translation with invented words («подтреесы», «переприменяйте»), inverted meanings («неизменённые изменения» and «неспециализированных изменений» both for "uncommitted changes"), calqued idioms («Со временем вы сделали ещё 2 коммита» for "You've since made"), and em-dashes glued to words («сценария—он сохраняет»). It also silently drops the EN scenario diagram in 3 of the 8 items that have one.
- Where the question bank is strong, it is strong for one reusable reason: every answer opens with a `###` heading that states the essence in plain words before the first sentence begins («Разовая настройка vs регулярная синхронизация», "Fixing the very last commit, nothing more", "Downloading vs downloading-and-merging"), then gives a lead sentence that answers directly, then code, then a **Common pitfall**. That four-part skeleton is why C scores 4 here against 3.0 in comparable banks, and it is the thing to copy into zones that lack it.

**Прочее:** The verdict splits by file: content/questions/git.json is close to `ok` (targeted E fixes — add real command output and two or three commit graphs — plus a handful of long senior sentences in q-17/q-19/q-20), while content/quiz/git.json needs a full rewrite, which is what drives the zone verdict to systemic-refactor. Neither `git` nor `event-driven` has an article, but Git suffers less: the question bank's per-entry `###` heading + lead + code + pitfall skeleton makes each card self-contained, which is exactly what a bank without an article needs. One factual inconsistency worth flagging to a subject reviewer, not a language pass: git-q-16 says reflog entries expire at ~90 days and dangling objects at ~30, while git-quiz-10 and git-quiz-19 both say 30 days for the same thing (Git's actual defaults are 90 / 30 / 14 for reflogExpire, reflogExpireUnreachable and pruneExpire).

### graphql (статьи+вопросы+quiz) — системный рефактор

- The zone has two completely different authors and the reader pays for the seam. The 14 articles are deep, cross-referenced and technically careful; the 30-question bank and 24-item quiz are template-generated at a fraction of the depth and repeatedly contradict the articles they sit next to. Concretely: article 03 states that top-level mutations MUST run serially, quiz-16 states it is 'common but not required'; article 04 states DataLoader turns N+1 into 2 queries, quiz-7 says 'a single batched query'; article 06 states HTTP caching is where REST wins, quiz-25 calls that statement false. A reader working the topic front to back is told opposite things within one session, and the quiz — the layer they meet last — is the one that is wrong.
- Generated content in this zone is padded by duplication instead of depth, and the duplication is mechanical enough to be measured. The question bank is 30 entries covering 15 topics, each asked exactly twice (1&6, 2&7, 3&8, 4&9, 5&10, 11&16, 12&17, 13&18, 14&19, 15&20, 21&26, 22&28, 23&27, 24&29, 25&30). The quiz is 24 items covering 6 concepts (Query vs Mutation x4, N+1 x5, fragments x4, Apollo cache x3, introspection x3, GraphQL vs REST x4, plus a missing id graphql-quiz-22). The duplicate slot is spent restating the first answer, so a bank that looks like 30 questions gives 15 topics at ~50 words each, and the senior tier ends up SHORTER (49 words) than the junior tier (72). The fix is not to lengthen sentences — it is to merge each pair into one answer at article depth and spend the freed slots on the senior material the articles cover but the bank never mentions: null bubbling, serial mutation execution, introspection, __resolveType, cursor/Relay pagination, @deprecated and additive evolution, query aliasing, BFF.
- Explanatory prose is routinely put inside code blocks. Across all 14 articles, ```txt is used as a general layout device: whole sections (Rate Limiting, Introspection, Authorization, Federation in article 05; every 'Связь с другими темами' and most 'Типичные follow-up' blocks) are body text in a monospace, non-reflowing block hard-wrapped at ~72 characters. For the target reader — phone, short bursts — this is the single most damaging habit in the zone, because it turns readable paragraphs into horizontally scrolling columns. ```txt should be reserved for the genuine ASCII diagrams (the Federation and BFF boxes), and the rest converted to ordinary markdown paragraphs and lists.
- Emphasis is done with CAPITAL LETTERS instead of markdown, at a density that reads as shouting and defeats tooling. en/01 has 8 instances in 431 prose words, en/02 6, and the habit runs through every article ('НЕ ВЫЗЫВАЮТСЯ', 'ВСЮ', 'ONE specification', 'THEIR REAL IMPACT', 'AT THE DATABASE LEVEL'). It is also why the flags script reports ONE, EVERY, INSIDE, THEIR, RESULT, AT as unexpanded abbreviations — false positives caused entirely by the style. Bold or italics carry the same emphasis without the cost.

**Прочее:** Quiz numbers requested: (a) correct option is strictly the longest in 21/24 items (en and ru; avg 17.8 words correct vs 12.8 distractor) — 'always pick the longest' scores 87.5%; (b) correctIndex distribution 0:21, 1:2 (items 3, 17), 2:1 (item 25), 3:0 — 'always pick A' also scores 87.5%, and 18 items are both index 0 AND longest; (c) 5 items whose explanation contradicts its own key, the articles or the bank: 21 (5000+ vs 51 queries), 16 (mutations 'not required' to be serial — contradicts spec, article 03, quiz-1, quiz-11, and makes distractor B true), 25 ('Option A is false' when A is true; contradicts quiz-15, quiz-20, article 06), 13 (its key is quiz-8's rejected distractor on cache-first), 7 ('N+1 into a single batched query' vs quiz-2 and article 04's 'N+1 to 2'); (d) 0 unedited generation artifacts — no 'Wait, let me recalculate' / 'I apologize' anywhere in the zone; (e) 9 items reference option positions (11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 21, 23, 24, 25 = 18 strings across both locales) — letters currently map correctly to file order, so they work in the topic-quiz route and are wrong by construction in the shuffled random-quiz route.
Bank verdict on substance: too thin, but the flag density (5.8/1k) is misleading — the prose is clean, the coverage is not. 30 entries = 15 topics x 2, senior answers average 49 words and shorter than junior's 72, and the zone's own articles list the exact answer the bank gives to q-6 ('Query и Mutation отличаются только семантически') as interview mistake #1.
Other non-readability defects found while reading, for whoever owns the content: q-25 and q-30 import createComplexityLimitRule from graphql-depth-limit (wrong package); q-24 passes ApolloServer plugins an object with a bare didResolveOperation instead of an array, and uses an 'apollo-client-id' header while its own duplicate q-29 uses the correct extensions.persistedQuery.sha256Hash; q-28 puts raw SDL inside a ```typescript block; article 05's complexity snippet mixes graphql-validation-complexity's createComplexityLimitRule with graphql-query-complexity's estimators option; en/01..en/07 lack the '<!-- verified -->' header that all 7 ru files carry.
Quantified for the style guide: 11/24 quiz items (both locales) have a stripped opening code fence leaving a bare 'graphql' line; 36 bank code blocks in 18/30 answers are mislabelled ```typescript; 5 bank answers glue the closing fence to the code, swallowing the interview-trap note; 14 no-space em-dashes in 13/30 ru answers; 9/30 ru bank headings in English Title Case; 3 different ru renderings of 'over-fetching' inside the quiz alone, plus the ungrammatical 'точное выбор полей' in quiz-10.

### http-rest (статьи+quiz) — точечные правки

- The articles are among the cleanest on the site on sentence length, lead sentences and concept density (B 4.35, C 3.7, D 4.5 — every new idea lands next to a diagram, table or code block), and the single repeating defect is abbreviations. An acronym is expanded in the one article whose title is about it and nowhere else: CORS is spelled out in 04 but bare in 01 and 09; SSE is spelled out by the heading in 08 but used bare four lines earlier in that same file's intro; HoL is expanded in 07 only. Meanwhile the transport-layer set (TCP, TLS, UDP, RTT, QUIC, CDN, DNS) is never expanded anywhere in the zone — RTT is used 11 times in 07 and 9 times in 09 without ever being written as 'round-trip time'. Fixing A is mechanical: one parenthetical at the first use per file, no restructuring.
- The quiz layer is built to a different (much lower) standard than everything around it and its defects are structural, not linguistic. Three independent tells let a reader score without knowing HTTP: the key is index 0 in 22/28 items and never 2 or 3; the correct option is the longest option in 14/28; and 10/28 items are near-verbatim repeats of an earlier item. On top of that the bank contradicts the articles it is supposed to test (409 vs 412 for If-Match, Server Push framed as a live advantage the article calls a failed feature) and skips three whole articles (REST principles, pagination, real-time) entirely. Article-level fixes are cosmetic; the quiz needs a rebuild against the article outline.
- Both localisations drift from each other in small, load-bearing ways rather than in register. The register is fine — RU is living language, EN is roughly B1-B2 — but each locale carries its own broken code example that the other has correct: RU 03 declares `(_req, res)` then reads `req.headers`, EN 04 has `"PUT", PATCH"` with a missing quote. RU 01 has a garbled phrase (`нафиксировано зачем`) where EN reads fine. In the quiz, the EN explanation for quiz-13 ends with `making option 1 the only correct behavior here` and the RU explanation silently drops that clause. Whatever pass produced these files did not diff the two locales against each other.

**Прочее:** Zone-specific finding requested: content/questions/postgresql.json is confirmed a later rewrite of content/questions/http-rest.json — q-1..q-15 are byte-identical, q-16..q-25 are rewritten 2.4x-3.4x longer and re-scoped (Richardson/HATEOAS, RFC 7807, circuit breaker, webhook signature verification replace the originals). The quiz aligns with NEITHER: it is shallower than the thin original (no pagination, no versioning, no rate limiting, no TLS handshake) and shares zero topics with the rewrite's senior half. Of the quiz's 28 items, 9 map to article 01, 6 to 03, 6 to 04, 4 to 07 (HTTP/2 only), 2 to 06, and 0 to articles 02, 05 and 08. It tests two things no article teaches: `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` being invalid in HTTP/2 (quiz-29 — Transfer-Encoding appears nowhere in 07), and 422 vs 409 for business-rule failures (quiz-24 — 422 gets one table row in 01 and is never contrasted with 409). No literal generation artifacts of the 'Wait, let me recalculate' kind exist in this bank; the artifacts here are structural — quiz-16 and quiz-29 print all four options verbatim inside the question stem, quiz-11 and quiz-22 carry stray code blocks unrelated to their options, explanations reference options 1-based while correctIndex is 0-based, and ids 21 and 26 are missing (28 items numbered 1-30).

### http-rest + postgresql(mislabelled) (вопросы) — системный рефактор

- Both files share one fixed answer shape in q-1..q-15: `### Heading` -> a single paragraph that fires every fact at once -> one code block at the very end -> a one-line pitfall. The example therefore always arrives AFTER all the theory and never between two concepts, so the reader has to hold three or four new terms (ETag + Last-Modified + Cache-Control + 304; token bucket + sliding window + fixed window + three X-RateLimit headers) with nothing to hold on to until the code appears. Density, not length, is what makes this tier hard: the answers are only ~57 prose words, but nothing in them is illustrated in place.
- Untranslated English is left inline in the Russian at three escalating severities, in both files. (1) Accepted loanwords used bare: fallback, retry, pipelining, push. (2) Unglossed jargon phrases treated as if Russian: head-of-line blocking, domain sharding, flow control, connection migration, early data, retry amplification, thundering herd, bulkhead, fingerprint, flight, span, trace, propagation. (3) Outright breakage: «статеф» (stateful), «problem двух генералов», «фрейминирование», «медленнеет», «сложнее в размышлении», «весь пользователя». Severity 3 is a copy-editing pass; severity 2 is the real readability tax, because the answer's key mechanism is named in a language the reader was not told they needed.
- The rewritten senior tier (postgresql.json q-16..q-25) fixed concept density by adding LENGTH but never by shortening sentences. It packs three or four facts per sentence, joined by em-dashes and nested parentheticals: 40.8% of EN sentences and 26.0% of RU sentences exceed the limit, up to 67 words. So the zone fails the rubric in two opposite directions at once — the thin tier is too dense per word, the rich tier is too long per sentence — and a single 'shorten it' or 'expand it' instruction will not fix both.
- EN is harder than RU in the rich tier, contrary to the usual +19% expectation being the only difference: 40.8% vs 26.0% of sentences over limit, and the EN adds idioms and phrasal verbs a B1-B2 reader will stall on that the RU does not have — 'hammer a downstream service', 'fire off dozens of requests', 'transient blips', 'which hop actually ate the latency', 'taking down checkout', 'doesn't scale horizontally for free', 'shipping a feature', 'trimmed this to 1 RTT', 'bakes the cryptographic handshake into', 'for the same fundamental reason two-generals-problem-style' (which is also ungrammatical).
- In both files the first sentence of an answer does answer the question, but frequently by compressing the ENTIRE answer into it, after which the following paragraphs re-say it in detail. The pyramid degenerates into 'abstract, then repeat' — e.g. http-rest-q-18 RU packs bidirectional/persistent-TCP/SSE-unidirectional/auto-reconnect/when-to-choose/overhead into five sentences that the code block then only partially illustrates. A lead should land one claim, not summarise six.

**Прочее:** DUPLICATION VERDICT: postgresql.json is neither a PostgreSQL bank nor a copy of http-rest.json. q-1..q-15 (junior+middle) are byte-identical in both files; all ten senior entries q-16..q-25 are a full rewrite with different question text, different topic coverage, and 3-4x longer answers (RU 80-140w -> 366-486w). So postgresql.json = http-rest.json's junior/middle tier + a rebuilt senior tier, and it is unambiguously the LATER draft: it switches to «ты» («Объясни» vs «Объясните»), uses the current site marker «Частая ловушка» / «Common pitfall» where http-rest.json still uses the older «Типичная ошибка» / «Common interview trap», and adds ASCII diagrams, nginx config and JSON payloads that http-rest.json's senior tier has none of.
Decisive content finding: http-rest.json's senior tier covers only FIVE distinct topics across its ten slots — q16≈q21 (HTTP/2 multiplexing), q18≈q23 (WebSockets/SSE), q19≈q24 (idempotency keys), q20≈q25 (OpenTelemetry tracing), q22 (HTTP/3) alone. The shared middle tier has the same defect in both files: q6≈q11 (ETag vs Last-Modified), q7≈q14 (pagination), q8≈q12 (API versioning), q9≈q13 (CORS), q10≈q15 (rate limiting). postgresql.json's rewrite fixes this for senior: ten distinct topics, adding TLS session resumption, Richardson Maturity Model / HATEOAS, RFC 7807, circuit breaker / bulkhead, and webhook HMAC signing.
WHICH FILE SHOULD SURVIVE: postgresql.json's CONTENT, re-labelled to http-rest.json. http-rest.json's q-16..q-25 should be dropped, not merged — every topic they cover is covered better in the rewrite, and merging would reimport the five duplicate pairs. Whichever file survives still needs the five middle-tier duplicate pairs collapsed, and a genuine PostgreSQL bank must be written from scratch: content/topics/postgresql exists, so that questions page is live and today serves HTTP/REST answers (src/lib/questions.ts:8 resolves `${topicId}.json` by filename and ignores the topicId field inside).
FLAG CORRECTION: the 'pitfall marker absent from 100% of answers' flag for http-rest.json is a FALSE NEGATIVE. All 25 answers do carry a pitfall block; it is just worded «Типичная ошибка:» / «Common interview trap:» instead of the site-standard «Частая ловушка:» / «Common pitfall:». The 57-prose-words-per-answer figure is real, however, and confirms the 'older, thinner template' hypothesis.
ARE THE THIN ANSWERS TOO THIN (rubric D)? For junior questions they work — PUT vs PATCH genuinely fits in 75 words plus code. For senior they do not: q21's whole treatment of when HTTP/2 stops helping is one 20-word sentence naming two unexplained mechanisms, and q22's QUIC example invents an `X-QUIC-Session` HTTP header that does not exist, so the code actively misteaches. Read side by side, http-rest.json's senior answers read as the SUMMARY of an answer the reader was never given. This is a D=2 for that file and the strongest argument for keeping the rewrite.

### javascript (вопросы) — системный рефактор

- The 'Common pitfall / Частая ловушка' closer is a fixed structural habit and a fixed defect: 128 of 129 answers end with one, 113 of those are a single sentence, and in EN 117 of 126 exceed the sentence limit (average 58 words, worst 111; RU average 34, worst 78). Because it is the last thing on screen it is the most-remembered slot in every answer, and it is reliably the hardest sentence in the answer. Fix pattern: state the mistake in one short sentence, then the consequence in a second, then the correct alternative in a third — the technical content already decomposes into exactly those three.
- Answers are built as 'label → code → explanation', and 11-12 of 129 never write the answer as prose at all: q-44, q-62, q-89, q-90 open with a raw code fence, and q-1, q-13, q-28, q-34, q-54 (en), q-71, q-100 open with a bolded section label that restates the question. A further group leads with the wrong thing on purpose: q-92 opens with the pre-ES2022 WeakMap workaround, q-98 with the recursive version that the question asks to replace, q-100 and q-114 with the problem rather than the answer. Rubric C would go from 3-4 to 5 by prepending one plain-words sentence — no other change needed.
- RU and EN are not the same text at two lengths — they are two different drafts. For q-1..q-109 the EN prose is 1.8× the RU (up to 3.9× at q-109), and the difference is almost entirely the consolidating paragraph that follows a code block and explains what just happened; RU deletes it. For q-110..q-129 the ratio is 1.05, i.e. a faithful translation. The result is that EN and RU fail different rubrics: EN carries the explanation but in 60-135-word sentences (B/F), while RU is crisp but has had the explanation removed (D) — including, at q-56, the one sentence that actually answers the question asked. Any fix pass has to decide 'restore into RU, then shorten in both', not treat one locale as the source of truth.
- RU quality splits sharply by difficulty tier. The junior/middle answers are clean, living Russian; the senior/advanced tier accumulates a layer of transliterated jargon that has no gloss and cannot be looked up — 'резолвится' (12×), 'вычищает очередь' as a calque of 'drain the queue' (16×), 'settle-ится' (7×), 'коэрсит' (6×), 'крашит/крашнуть' (7×), 'yield-нуть', plus calques like 'чиста для написания' and 'не подлежащий сборке мусора namespace'. Notably the classic bureaucratic markers are absent (2× «является», zero «осуществляется»/«данный»), so this is a jargon problem, not a register problem.

**Прочее:** Three code examples are genuinely broken in both locales, not just hard to read: an unescaped \n in the JSON turned into a real newline at q-17 (the multi-line-string example now shows an unterminated single-quoted string spanning three lines, demonstrating the opposite of its point), q-124 (`.join('` split across lines) and q-127 (`// "a` split across lines). Worth fixing before any language pass. Separately, q-81 explains stale closures using useState/useEffect without saying it is React or what a dependency array is — the only place in the bank where an answer depends on a framework the reader may not know. 293 EN / 272 RU code lines exceed 92 characters, nearly all because of right-aligned trailing comments that will wrap on a phone anyway.

### javascript (статьи+quiz) — точечные правки

- POSITIVE — the house structure of articles 01-12 is the best on the site and should be lifted verbatim into the style guide: (1) every section opens with a one-sentence plain claim and no warm-up («Замыкание = функция + ссылка на Environment Record», «`this` — это не переменная»), (2) a ```txt ASCII diagram or a numbered spec algorithm comes within 2-3 lines of the claim, before any second idea, (3) a runnable code block with the expected value written as an inline `// comment` on the same line follows immediately, (4) each article ends with the same two fixed sections — «Связь с другими темами» (a txt block of cross-links) and «Типичные ошибки на интервью» (quoted myth → нет/no → correction). The result is that theory never runs more than ~4 sentences before an example, which is why D and E average 4.8 here versus much lower in other zones.
- POSITIVE — the myth-first bullet («"Хойстинг поднимает код наверх"» — код не перемещается…) is the single most reusable device in the zone: it states what the reader probably believes, refutes it in one word, then gives the mechanism. It appears 6-7 times per article and is why C averages 4.8. Two conditions make it work and must be written into the guide: the quoted claim must be FALSE (ru/07 breaks this and answers «да»), and the refutation must be the second or third word, not buried.
- POSITIVE — abbreviations that ARE expanded are expanded by structure, not by parenthesis: the spec term gets its own H2/H3 in full («Temporal Dead Zone — что реально происходит», «Environment Records — что за ними стоит») and the short form is used only afterwards. The failures listed in unexpanded_abbrevs are almost all cases where the short form leaked into an earlier file section or into an ASCII diagram before that heading arrived (TDZ at line 46 of article 01, GC in the article 09 lifecycle diagram).
- NEGATIVE — the RU locale is the second-class citizen wherever the two versions diverged. Every divergence found goes the same direction: EN fixed, RU stale. ru/07 keeps the broken myth bullet EN repaired; ru/08 keeps the `createLogger` example that references a variable declared later, which EN rewrote; ru/12 names a variable `byLength` while grouping by parity, which EN renamed to `byParity`; ru/13 prints «Ответ: `3, 1, 4, 2`» in the open where en/13 hides every answer in `<details><summary>Answer</summary>`, so the RU self-test is spoiled before it is attempted. RU also carries four garbled words that no proofreader saw («Семь простанство», «трансп», «полупривате», «Оrinoco» with a Cyrillic О).
- NEGATIVE — the quiz bank was clearly authored separately from the articles and never reconciled with them: it says `var` has a TDZ (article 01 says the opposite in bold), it puts Rendering after Macrotasks (article 05's diagram puts it between them), and RU uses the transliterations «Микротаски/Макротаски» where all thirteen RU articles use «микрозадачи/макрозадачи». The bank also refers to distractors by index («Вариант 2», «Option 0», «Option B») in three mutually incompatible schemes, none of which the reader can see on screen. The articles never do this.

**Прочее:** Longest-option count (exact): the correct option is strictly the longest in 14/47 items (en) and 12/47 (ru); tied-longest in a further 5. Mean length correct 41.9 vs distractor 35.1 chars (en). This is a mild pull, nothing like quiz/postgresql — in 16/47 items the correct option is the (tied) shortest. correctIndex (exact): 0 in 26/47, 1 in 19/47, 2 in 1/47, 3 in 1/47 — so 45 of 47 answers sit in the first two slots and the last two slots are effectively decorative. This is the postgresql/nestjs failure mode and needs a reshuffle, not a rewrite. Two factual staleness items outside the readability remit: quiz-28 says an unhandled rejection lets execution continue (Node >=15 exits by default), and ru/11 + en/11 say `require()` can never load ESM (Node >=22.12 supports require(esm)).

### kafka (статьи) — точечные правки

- Article 02 is written as the zone's glossary — every Kafka noun gets a bold lead definition — and articles 03, 05, 06 and 07 then silently inherit it and define nothing of their own. 03 opens with «в какой из N партишнов топика его записать» (topic, partition, producer bare); 05 uses producer/broker/consumer/offset/acks/ISR bare; 06 and 07 use consumer group, retention, replay, throughput, at-least-once bare. The load-bearing case is `lag`: it is the punchline of a section in 03, 05 and 07, and defined in none of them (only in 04 and 08). This is the site-wide failure mode, confirmed here: a reader arriving from search into 03, 05, 06 or 07 gets no definitions at all.
- Layout and density invert exactly at the interview file. Articles 01-07 hold D=5 because every new idea is immediately followed by a txt diagram — this zone's strongest asset. Article 08 (2714 RU / 2896 EN words) has one code block and zero diagrams, 25-27 over-long paragraphs and the zone's longest sentences (RU 59w, EN 68w). Because the kafka topic has no question bank and no quiz, 08 is the reader's only retrieval-practice surface and is the one file formatted as a wall.
- The RU layer is not fully translated below the H1. English survives inside Russian diagrams and prose («Это bottleneck», «Faster controller failover», «event-driven retention», «Dead Letter Queue for failed messages», «discovery кластера», «network blip», «а не чистым техническим fit»), and English verbs get Russian endings («ревокают», «ревокации», «мониторится», «батчить»). Two of these are outright errors: «нефриптографическая» (03) and «ту же партишну» / «фундаментальная компромисс» (08 / 01).
- EN is harder than RU wherever the flags cluster, and not only because it is longer. EN 01 has 10.9% long sentences against RU's 1.5%; EN 08 11.6% against RU's 4.3%. EN also introduces C1 vocabulary that has no RU counterpart in the same slot: 'going sideways', 'quibble', 'commodity hardware', 'headroom', 'provision', 'canonical', 'forfeits', 'spin up', 'wired directly', 'retroactively'.

**Прочее:** RU 06's H1 «Kafka vs RabbitMQ» is fine as-is (both are product names, «vs» is standard in RU tech writing) — the real untranslated layer is inside the RU diagrams, see pattern 3. Kafka/06 heavily duplicates content/topics/rabbitmq/ru|en/05-rabbitmq-vs-alternatives.md (both cover log-vs-queue, dumb/smart broker, replay, routing, cloud managed options) and the two disagree twice: rabbitmq/05 lists «Exactly-once semantics с Kafka транзакциями» as a plain Kafka strength while kafka/05 and kafka/08 insist it holds only Kafka→Kafka; and rabbitmq/05 rates RabbitMQ at «~50k–150k сообщений/сек на ноду» while kafka/06 says it «отлично справляется с сотнями тысяч сообщений в секунду». Cross-zone RU terminology also clashes: kafka uses «партишн»/«consumer», rabbitmq uses «партиция»/«потребитель» — for a reader following the cross-reference these read as different concepts. Two factual slips noticed in passing, outside the readability remit: ru/04 and en/04 call `idempotent: true` «настройка брокера» / «broker-side setting» (it is a producer client option), and ru/04:390 leaves a dead destructure `const { CONNECT, DISCONNECT, REQUEST_TIMEOUT } = consumer.events;` that the EN version already removed.

### keycloak-auth (статьи) — системный рефактор

- ALL-CAPS is the zone's default emphasis device, and it is used 228 times in prose alone across the 22 files (plus more inside the ASCII diagram blocks): EN shouts WANTS / GOT / WHAT / WHO / EVERY / SAME / ENTIRE / MUST / ON TOP / SIMULTANEOUSLY, RU shouts ХОЧЕТ / КАЖДЫЙ / НИКОГДА / АБСОЛЮТНО / ВООБЩЕ / ОДНОЙ / МЕХАНИЗМ. Because everything is emphasized, nothing is — and on a phone it reads as an angry voice. It also corrupts the tooling: a large share of the script's 344 'unexpanded abbreviations' for this zone are these caps words (EVERY, GOT, WHO, TOP, WANTS, BEFORE, OLD, WHICH…), not acronyms. Fix: **bold** for the load-bearing word, caps only for real acronyms and literal config values (SAMEORIGIN, S256).
- The zone's default sentence shape is 'lead clause — em-dash — second independent clause — parenthetical containing a cross-reference to another article — em-dash — consequence', carrying three or four facts. This is why EN runs 43-60% of sentences over 25 words (file 06 at 60%, with a 98-word sentence) and RU 28-45% over 28 words. The parenthetical cross-references are the main accelerant: nearly every explanatory paragraph carries one or two '(see article 0X)' / '(статья 0X)' asides, which both lengthen the sentence and interrupt exactly the reader the site targets — someone reading in short bursts. Fix: one fact per sentence; move the cross-reference to its own short sentence at the end of the paragraph.
- Almost every acronym is spelled out exactly once, in the article that introduces the concept, and then used bare in the other ten files. PKCE is expanded in 01 and used 9× bare in 07; JWKS is expanded in 03 and used 5× bare in 04; XSS is used 8× in 06 (the article whose whole argument rests on it) and never expanded; TTL appears 5× in 03 and 4× in 11 unexpanded. Since files are read out of order, the first use in each file needs a three-word gloss. The cheatsheet (10) and the question bank (11) are worst hit — 20 and 30 bare acronyms respectively.
- The ru locale carries machine-translation residue that a reader will notice: six English words spliced into Russian sentences ('over логированием' 04:20, 'either … либо' 03:318, 'even если' 05:102, 'requires БД lookup' 03:133, 'не safer по умолчанию' 06:76, 'architectural дефект' 06:179), four mixed-alphabet typos ('raньше' 01:300, 'upскорить' 03:141, 'статeless' 04:329, 'Chuжой' 07:62), and one mistranslated core term ('Резервный сервер' for Resource Server, 01:130). A single grep pass over the ru files for Latin-script function words and for words mixing Cyrillic with Latin letters would catch all eleven.
- Every one of the nine conceptual articles opens with a meta section ('Зачем без этого нельзя…' / 'Why you can't write secure auth code without this', 'Зачем разбираться в модели, а не сразу лезть в код') that spends two or three paragraphs justifying the article before stating a single fact. Section-level leads inside the articles are good (definition first, caveats after) — it is specifically the article opener that makes the reader scroll past positioning to reach content. Fix: one sentence of 'what this article answers', then the first real claim.

**Прочее:** Depth and structure are the zone's strength and should not be touched: diagram/code rhythm is genuinely good (theory_walls=0 in articles 01-10), and the trade-off framing (honest 'X isn't free' sections) is exactly right for the target reader. Two non-language defects worth a ticket anyway: the code snippets for UmaPermissionGuard (04) and StepUpGuard (08) use this.reflector without injecting it, in both locales, so they don't compile; and file 10's grant-type table has five cells in a four-column row while its Part 2 comparison rows run to 661 characters (ru) / 423 (en). ASCII diagrams run 79-137 characters wide (01's discovery JSON is 137) and the outer boxes in 01 and 02 have misaligned right borders — both hurt the phone reader the rubric describes.

### microfrontends (статьи) — системный рефактор

- The zone's dominant sentence shape is a 40-90 word 'fact sandwich': claim — em-dash — nested parenthetical qualification — second em-dash — consequence. It is used for every important idea in all 16 files, so the reader's hardest sentence is always the one carrying the load-bearing point. Mechanically: 269 over-long sentences at 23.0/1k words, peaking at 45.8% of sentences in en/06 and 42.6% in en/07. Breaking each of these into claim / detail / consequence sentences would fix the single biggest readability cost in the zone without touching a fact.
- `MFE` is expanded exactly once, in article 01, and then used bare in all seven other files including the question bank — and the same habit applies to CDN, CI/CD, E2E, TTFB, SEO, DOM, BEM, CSSOM, SSI and REST/gRPC. The articles are written as a linear book (they also cross-reference each other as 'article 03', 'статья 06'), but they are read as standalone pages. Every file needs its own first-use expansion.
- Russian is a partly-finished translation of the English rather than an independent text: an untranslated `result:` survives in ru/05, `publичит` in ru/03, `не satisfied` twice in ru/03, «одну единственную источник правды» / «одна источник правды» (agreement error tracing 'a single source of truth') in ru/04 and ru/08, plus raw transliterations «блэст-радиус», «лок-степе», «гейтованного feature-флагом», «коллизирует», «неймспейс-незащищённый». Latin words also sit inside Russian syntax as ordinary parts of speech («когда происходит resolution», «cost автономии vs сложности»).
- The question bank (article 08) is the structural weak point: 17 answers, 23 over-long paragraphs, 4 theory walls, and zero diagrams or tables even though the seven source articles it summarises all have them. Where article 03 gives the share-scope algorithm as a numbered 5-step list, article 08 flattens it back into a single 140-word prose block; the shared config code block is even reproduced with all of article 03's explanatory comments stripped out. Summarising should not mean removing the scaffolding.

**Прочее:** Overlap with nx-monorepo ch.09-11 is near-total for topic article 03 (host/remote/container, remoteEntry, share scope, singleton/strictVersion/eager, the bootstrap async boundary, 'Invalid hook call') — worth a deliberate split of scope plus cross-links, since neither side references the other.
Two places where the course is the *better* text and the topic reads as vague by comparison: (1) course ch.11 states the deterministic rule 'the first one to load wins' on singleton version drift and quotes the exact console warning; topic 03 Scenario 2 only says the runtime 'may pick a version the remote team never tested against'. (2) course ch.11 reconciles `eager: true` and `import('./bootstrap')` as two alternative cures; topic 03 presents both as required, 60 lines apart (see worst_places entry 6).
Diagnostics differ without explanation: topic 03 recommends `window.__webpack_share_scopes__.default`, course ch.11 recommends `__REACT_DEVTOOLS_GLOBAL_HOOK__.renderers.size`. React versions also differ (topic pins ^18.2.0 throughout, course uses 18.3/^19).
One code-example defect worth a fix pass: the contract test in article 07 uses `render` and `React.ComponentProps` without importing either, and its actual mechanism (the type annotation is the contract check; the runtime `not.toThrow()` is not) is uncommented — a junior will read the assertion as the test.

### mongodb-mongoose (статьи) — системный рефактор

- The untranslated layer in ru goes three levels deep, not one. (1) 8 of 9 H1s are English — only 09 is translated. (2) Every cross-reference inside Russian prose is an English article title: «см. [Indexes and Query Performance]», «см. [Mongoose Queries, populate, and Pitfalls]» — 5-8 per file, always mid-sentence. (3) Every article closes with a «Связь с другими темами» block whose entire left column is English titles glossed in Russian, so the last screen a Russian reader sees is a bilingual table. Translating only the H1s would leave roughly 45 English article titles per file still embedded in Russian sentences, and the closing block untouched. The same habit continues at word level with inflected English: «два honest-подхода», «trade-off локальности индекса», «rolling-способом», «IP не в whitelist», «лечится healthcheck по readyState».
- Article 09 is the zone's single point of failure, and it fails by dropping the very scaffolding articles 01-08 use well. This topic has no question bank and no quiz, so 09 is the reader's actual interview-prep surface — and it is the only file with no code block, table or diagram inside any answer: 26 paragraphs of 175-240 words, 7 theory runs of 570-900 words, and every code example demoted to inline backticks inside a prose sentence (a full four-argument `findOneAndUpdate(...)` call inside answer 11). Articles 01-08 solve exactly this problem — a diagram, table or code block every two to three paragraphs, which is why their D average is 4.9. Answer 25 (four production requirements, 230 words, one paragraph) and answer 18 (write concern plus read concern plus read preference, 225 words) are the two places to fix first: the material they compress is already presented well in 08 and 06 with a table and a numbered list respectively.
- Acronyms are treated as shared vocabulary, and the pattern is specifically about the unguessable ones. COLLSCAN and IXSCAN are the working currency of articles 04, 05 and 08 and are glossed exactly once in the zone (the opening line of 04); a reader landing on 03 or 08 first meets COLLSCAN as the payload of a warning with no gloss at all. N+1 is never expanded anywhere, although the populate section's whole argument is to correct the reader's understanding of it. WiredTiger is named in 03, 04, 06 and 09 as the reason a document rewrite is expensive and is never once introduced as MongoDB's storage engine. Add 3NF, EAV, GIN, DDL, FK, GDPR, DTO, BI, IoT, OOM and NoSQL — none expanded on first use in any file — plus «eventual consistency», «hash join / merge join» and «capped-коллекция» used as if already known.
- About a dozen sections open with a fenced block instead of a lead sentence, which inverts the pyramid the rest of the zone follows well: «## Unique, partial, TTL» → ```js; «## Read concern: какие данные считать существующими» → ```txt; «## Обработка ошибок: маппинг в ответ API» → a table; also «## Single field», «## Операторы выборки», «## Основные стадии», «## Read preference», «## Write concern», «## explain(): как читать план», «## SchemaTypes и приведение типов», «## strict mode», «## autoIndex». The reader arriving from a table of contents gets syntax before purpose. Everywhere else the leads are genuinely strong (the «Проблема: … решение:» pattern in 03 is the best in the zone), which is what makes the gaps conspicuous — the fix is one sentence per section, not a restructure.
- en is measurably harder than ru in every file, and the gap widens with length: share of over-limit sentences en/ru is 24%/12% (01), 11%/1% (03), 19%/9% (04), 19%/8% (07), 12%/4% (08), 31.5%/15% (09). en also carries the register that ru renders plainly — «a grown-up answer», «a bolt-on», «a lifeline, not an operating mode», «races the candidates over a small amount of work», «buys denormalization», «analytics and BI trip over», «above the fold», «taking that rule to absurdity», «hunting for copies» — and the widest ASCII tables (116 columns in en/08, 106 in en/01) because English fills more cells. Any language pass should be sequenced en-first: the ru text is already close, the en text is where the target reader loses the thread.

**Прочее:** Content bug, not a readability finding: ru/08 «вернётся ДОкументное состояние» is a corrupted sentence (en/08 has the correct «the state BEFORE the change») — worth fixing before any style pass. Narrow-screen widths inside fenced blocks: en/08 116 cols, ru/08 110, en/01 106, ru/01 96, en/03 91, en/04 and en/06 89; files 02, 05 and 09 stay under 80 throughout, so a workable width already exists in the zone's own style. ALL-CAPS emphasis is restrained here (0-3 shouted words per file in 01-08, ~20 in 09) — unlike other zones this is not the dominant problem. Zone strengths to protect in any rewrite: the pyramid section leads, the diagram-per-concept density (D 4.39), the running blog example shared across all nine articles, and the «Типичные ошибки на интервью» closers, which are the best-written prose in the zone.

### nestjs (статьи+вопросы+quiz) — системный рефактор

- The articles put the explanation inside the code, not in prose. 48 of the 67 sections across the 10 ru articles (and the same 48 in en) go straight from an `##` heading into a fenced block, with no sentence in between; the definitions of Middleware, Guard, Pipe, Provider Scopes, forRoot/forFeature, Saga and CQRS handlers exist only as `//` comments. Prose is 62-77% code by word count in every one of the 20 files (prose: 230-410 words per article), and in file 10 eleven of eighteen Q items have no prose answer at all — only a code block. Result: rubric C collapses (avg 2.3) not because the lead sentences warm up, but because in most sections there is no lead sentence to judge.
- The zone reads as written for someone who already works in Nest. The very first sentence of the very first article depends on Guard, Interceptor, Exception Filter, transport and RPC, none introduced; DI is in the title of article 03 and is never expanded anywhere in the zone; RxJS/Observable carry all of article 05 without a word of introduction. There is no article on modules/controllers/providers, so no file establishes the vocabulary the other nineteen assume — and the rubric only counts expansions in the same file anyway. A avg 2.4.
- The Russian side is a partial translation rather than a Russian text. 15 headings are fully English, including 6 of the 10 article titles; article 09 opens with the half-translated "NestJS abstracts communication за унифицированным API"; article 07 has "overhead на GC" and "Performance чеклист"; article 10 has "топологический sort" and "GC nightmare". The quiz adds calques («что является основной разницей», «какое ожидаемое поведение») and terminology drift for the same concept — provider is «провайдер» in 14 places and «поставщик» in 3, scope is «scope» / «область» / «область видимости поставщика» depending on the item. G avg 2.7.
- The question bank is the opposite shape: its leads are excellent (C 4, only nestjs-q-22 opens with a code block instead of a sentence) but the sentences are long. 238 of 478 en sentences and 185 of 485 ru sentences exceed the threshold, the pitfall paragraph at the end of nearly every one of the 50 entries is a single 55-100-word sentence carrying three or four facts, and the en version is systematically harder than the ru one in both length and register ("the odd one out", "hammer us", "bolted onto", "racy read-then-write", "tanking throughput").
- The quiz has structural defects independent of language, in three layers: (a) the answer is option 0 in 26 of 28 items, so "always pick the first one" scores 93%; (b) the correct option is the longest in 19 of 28 en items and 17 of 28 ru — less extreme than quiz/postgresql's 26 of 29, but still roughly 2.5x chance, with the correct option averaging 1.3x the mean option length and reaching 1.9x in nestjs-quiz-24; (c) 28 items cover about six distinct facts — Guard vs Interceptor four times (1, 6, 16, 26), providers vs exports four times (4, 10, 25, 28), Pipes vs Filters three times (13, 20, 30), lifecycle hook order six times (5, 8, 15, 19, 23, 29) — and touch none of what the articles actually teach (ExecutionContext, Reflector, custom decorators, dynamic modules, CQRS, microservices, AsyncLocalStorage).

**Прочее:** Contradiction defect: CONFIRMED, twice. quiz-2's correct option says TRANSIENT gives a new instance per request, contradicting bank q-11, article 03, article 07 and quiz-17 (which marks the opposite behaviour correct); quiz-5's explanation puts onApplicationBootstrap after listen(), contradicting bank q-17 and article 10. quiz-12's explanation repeats the TRANSIENT error. Longest-option defect: present but milder than in quiz/postgresql (19/28 en, 17/28 ru vs 26/29); the far worse bias is positional — correctIndex is 0 in 26 of 28. Ids jump (11, 21 missing), so the bank is 28 items with 30 ids. Factual/E issue outside the readability remit: `new InjectionToken<string>(...)` imported from '@nestjs/common' is Angular's API, not Nest's, and appears in ru/en articles 03, 04 and 10 as a recommended practice. Also unrelated to my zone but noted: articles 03 and 07 both teach scope bubble-up with near-identical prose and code, and article 10's group 1/4 duplicate articles 03/07 wholesale.

### nextjs (вопросы) — системный рефактор

- The bank is really two banks with different writing rules, and the seam is the difficulty boundary. Entries q-1..q-54 open with an `### Heading` and a short lead that lands the answer, and carry 2-4 code blocks each. Entries q-55..q-70 (all `advanced`) have no heading at all, open with a bold label ('**Self-hosted/Docker:**', '**Модель Pages Router:**', '**Структура:**', '**Механика selective hydration:**') or a 40-58 word mechanism sentence, run 370-520 words, and eight of the sixteen contain no code, diagram or table whatsoever. The ru side additionally switches the reader's address form from «вы» to «ты» at exactly the same seam, including in the question texts. Any fix pass should treat q-55..q-70 as one job: add the answer-first heading, add the missing example or table, unify the address form.
- Answers habitually open on the contrast instead of the answer: the old world ('До PPR решение…', 'В традиционном долгоживущем сервере на Node.js…', '**Модель Pages Router:** на каждый запрос…'), the naive approach ('Это можно было бы наивно сымитировать через `useState`'), or why the obvious thing fails ('Почему "сгенерировать всё" не работает на таком масштабе'). The real answer then arrives one or two paragraphs later. This affects at least q-36, q-40, q-47, q-50, q-52, q-53, q-54, q-59, q-60, q-64, q-69. The contrast is usually worth keeping — it just belongs after a one-sentence direct answer, not instead of it.
- Every entry ends with a '**Частая ловушка / Common pitfall:**' block written as exactly one sentence, and those are the longest sentences in the bank: 6 of the 8 longest en sentences (99w, 89w, 88w, 87w, 85w, 83w) and 3 of the 8 longest ru ones are pitfall blocks. The content is valuable and should stay; the shape (one sentence carrying a three-item list, a parenthetical, an em-dash pivot and a closing comparison) should become three or four sentences. This is the single highest-leverage mechanical fix in the zone: it is a fixed template applied 70 times in each locale.
- Roughly thirty abbreviations are never expanded in either locale, and the most important one is the most used: RSC appears 11 times across six entries and is never written out as React Server Components, even though 'RSC payload' is load-bearing for the whole App Router half of the bank. Because a question bank is read card by card, 'explained in an earlier entry' is even weaker here than in an article series — ISR and CLS are expanded on first use and then reused bare a dozen entries later, which is the right instinct applied only once.

**Прочее:** Only two comparison tables exist in 70 entries (q-36, q-41) and both are excellent and phone-readable — the natural fix for the theory walls in q-59, q-63, q-64, q-65 and q-68 is already in the bank's own style. Code examples are the clear strength: short, self-contained, commented at non-obvious lines, no dependence on a previous entry's variables; the only real defect is q-51, where the section titled 'The Mistake'/'Ошибка' shows the correct snippet and the fix section repeats it verbatim. En is measurably harder than ru, not just longer: 54.4% of en sentences exceed 25 words vs 40.8% of ru sentences over 28, and en leans on idiom a B1-B2 reader will stall on ('trips people up', 'hand-roll', 'reach for' 10x, 'say-so', 'a blunt fallback', 'cross-origin-in-spirit', 'wire up', 'tear down', 'under the hood' 7x).

### nextjs (статьи) — точечные правки

- MOST IMPORTANT — abbreviations are expanded in the article that OWNS them and nowhere else. Article 02 correctly expands CSR/SSR/SSG/ISR in its H2 headings; article 07 correctly expands CLS, FOUT, FOIT; article 09 correctly defines the big four in its numbered answers. But article 01 — the entry point that a new reader opens FIRST — uses SSR 9×, SSG 6×, SPA 5×, plus CSR/ISR/RSC/SEO/TTFB/FCP/TTI/CLS/DOM/CRA/FOIT/FOUT/SWR and expands not one of them. Same shape in 04 (RSC in the very first code block, never expanded), 07 (LCP used 6× in prose, expanded 45 lines later in a table), 09 (CLS/LCP/INP used in Q54-55, defined in Q56). The habit is 'it's explained in the article about it', which the rubric explicitly rejects — and the fix is mechanical: move the existing expansion to the first mention in each file.
- The EN files are systematically harder than the RU files, and the cause is structural, not lexical: the RU sentence pattern 'claim — mechanism (parenthetical caveat) — consequence' joined by em-dashes survives translation intact, and English's extra articles and prepositions push it over the limit. Long-sentence rates: ru/06 6.1% vs en/06 31.9%; ru/07 26.8% vs en/07 40.5%; ru/04 15.4% vs en/04 30.8%. Worst single sentences are 66w (en/07 next-font), 56w (en/09 loading/error), 52w (en/06 template). Fix: at translation time, break every em-dash chain into separate sentences instead of preserving it.
- Every RU file has an English or code-switched H1: 5 are fully English (`# Next.js Fundamentals`, `# Rendering Models: CSR, SSR, SSG, ISR`, `# App Router vs Pages Router`, `# Server Components vs Client Components`, `# Next.js Interview Questions (Middle → Senior)`) and the other 4 are hybrids glued with «и» (`# Data Fetching, Caching и Revalidation`, `# Routing, Layouts и Middleware`, `# SEO, Metadata и Performance`, `# Production Architecture и Best Practices`). The pattern extends into H2s: `## Practical пример: e-commerce страница товара` (ru/05), `## Client Component — explicit opt-in` (ru/04), `## Четыре уровня кеширования в Next.js — must-know для senior` (ru/05).
- Three RU files contain raw untranslated English words wedged into Russian grammar — «— это means:» (ru/07), «Нюанс specific для App Router» (ru/08), «было source of truth для» where the EN says 'root cause' (ru/05) — plus one Latin letter inside a Cyrillic word, «крауlер» (ru/09), and a missing space after a comma («сборки**,self-host'ит», ru/07). These are not stylistic anglicisms, they are un-proofread machine-translation residue. They cluster in files 05, 07, 08, 09 — i.e. the later half of the topic, which suggests the pass ran out of attention.
- Sections tend to open with interview meta-framing rather than the fact: `## Уровень вопросов` / `## The level of these questions` (08, a paragraph about who asks these questions before any architecture), `## Четыре уровня кеширования — must-know для senior` opening with «Один из самых частых senior-вопросов…» (05), `## Контекст` / `## Context` opening with history about the Pages Router in an article about the App Router (03). The rest of the zone gets this right — ru/04 opens with `## SSR ≠ Server Components — главное, что нужно развести в голове` and answers immediately, which is the model the other files should follow.

**Прочее:** Strengths worth protecting: D (4.0) and E (3.8) are genuinely good — nearly every new concept lands on a code block or a `txt` diagram within a line or two, examples are short, self-contained and commented at the non-obvious line, and the model-comparison tables in 02/03/07/08 are excellent for phone reading. Do not touch those. Verdict is `targeted-fixes` rather than `systemic-refactor` because no restructuring is needed: the required edits are (1) an abbreviation-first-use pass per file, (2) an EN sentence-splitting pass, (3) nine H1 translations, (4) five named RU translation artifacts. That said, criterion B on the EN half (avg 2.4) is borderline systemic — all nine EN files need the sentence pass, not a handful of places. Two technical inconsistencies noticed in passing, outside the readability scope: ru+en/05 call `cookies()` synchronously while ru+en/02 teach that it became async in Next.js 15; ru+en/04 use `useState` in `ClientWrapper` without importing it, though the `Counter` example two blocks earlier does import it.

### nextjs-quiz (quiz) — системный рефактор

- The strongest position bias of the three banks and possibly of the site. correctIndex is 0 in 29 of 30 items — the single exception is nextjs-quiz-26 — and the correct option is strictly the longest in 24 of 30. On the per-topic route, where shuffleOptions is not applied, a reader who always picks the first, longest answer scores 29/30 without reading a single question. The shape is visible in the data too: correct options carry two or three coordinated clauses ("automatically resizes and serves optimized formats (WebP) based on device, preventing layout shift with aspect ratio control") while distractors are single claims.
- Half the bank asks four questions. Six items are "why use next/image instead of <img>" (4, 9, 14, 19, 25, 29) with near-identical correct options; three are "what is middleware for" (10, 23, 30); five are ISR/fetch caching (2, 8, 18, 24, 27); three are Server vs Client Component (1, 6, 15). The repetition is where the contradictions live — items 6 and 17 give opposite verdicts on bundle-size reduction, items 11 and 27 give opposite verdicts on getStaticProps, and five caching items state a v14 default that the zone's own article documents as changed in v15. Meanwhile Server Actions, streaming/Suspense, parallel and intercepting routes, error boundaries, metadata and generateMetadata get zero items.
- Russian is machine output that was never opened. Eight items carry tokens that exist in no language: «переvalidation», «переvalidates», «переvalidate» (six items, including one in a question stem and two in keyed-correct options), «переваиливаются», «теку». The English side of the same items is clean, so this is a translation pass that shipped without a proof-read — and it lands hardest on `revalidate`, the single most important word in a Next.js caching quiz.

**Прочее:** Scores are per locale for the whole bank. E is scored 2 rather than 3 because three of thirty stems (8, 21, 26) render their code as prose for want of a ``` fence, and 17's snippet throws at runtime. G is scored 1 because the artifacts are in keyed-correct options and question stems, not just prose, so they block answering, not merely reading. No item lacks a correct option and no model self-talk was found. Item ids are contiguous 1-30, unlike the react and nodejs banks. nextjs-quiz-28's explanation ends "This combines static generation with type safety" — type safety is unrelated to generateStaticParams and to everything else in the item.

### nodejs (вопросы) — системный рефактор

- The dominant structural habit: the opening paragraph packs a whole reference list into ONE colon-led sentence. 17 RU and 20 EN answers have a lead-paragraph sentence over 35 words built as 'X: a (aside), b (aside), c (aside)' — up to 85 words and six items (nodejs-q-42, q-34, q-67, q-77, q-78, q-50, q-94, q-100). The direct answer is usually present, so rubric C is not the problem; the problem is that it is welded to a six-item enumeration the reader must hold in memory before the first full stop. Fix: keep the one-line direct answer as its own sentence, then break the enumeration into a numbered or bulleted list — no technical content is lost, and these answers already use bold labels that map straight onto list items.
- The bank is two documents with two different quality levels. 73 answers close with «Частая ловушка / Common pitfall» and follow a disciplined shape (2 prose paragraphs → code → 1 summary paragraph → pitfall) in fluent Russian. The other 23 (nodejs-q-21..28, q-36..41, q-51..58) close with «Типичная ошибка на интервью / Common interview trap» and are visibly weaker in the same three ways every time: (a) no summary paragraph after the code, so the answer stops at the code and jumps to the pitfall; (b) Russian with dropped subjects and missing commas before subordinate clauses, reading as a machine translation of the EN («возвращает `true` если буфер ниже порога», «слушателя который авто-удаляется», «Предположение что...»); (c) the H3 heading narrows the answer to an advanced sub-angle and the lead answers that angle instead of the question above it — worst case nodejs-q-51, which is asked which event loop phase handles timers and never says.
