- EN is systematically harder than RU rather than equivalent: +13% words (21262 vs 18742) and 47% of EN sentences over 25 words against 33% of RU sentences over 28. Every borderline RU sentence lands over the EN limit, and EN additionally reaches for idiom where RU stays plain: 'wait out its timeout', 'ties up a connection/thread', 'the nuclear option', 'blast radius', 'exfiltrate', 'post-hoc', 'a network blip', 'strictly worse', 'sawtooth'. A language pass on EN should start by mirroring RU's sentence boundaries, not by rewording.

**Прочее:** The 23 answers without the «Частая ловушка / Common pitfall» marker do NOT end abruptly — they use the older wording «Типичная ошибка на интервью / Common interview trap», so all 96 have a closing block; the inconsistency is editorial, not a missing section (see pattern 2 for what is actually wrong with that batch). nodejs-q-29 is locale-inconsistent: RU «Частая ловушка», EN 'Common interview trap'. Real typo in nodejs-q-7 RU: «несбро шенные записи» (broken word). The digest's longest-sentence word counts are inflated — periods inside code spans like `process.nextTick()` defeat its sentence splitter, so its 154w/132w records for nodejs-q-48 are three sentences merged; my own counts (max 89w EN, 83w RU) are the real figures, and the 24.2/1k density still holds. The single theory wall it flags (nodejs-q-93) is fine: it is a four-flag reference list after a code block, not undigested theory.

### nodejs (статьи) — системный рефактор

- ALL-CAPS is the zone's default emphasis marker, and it is used to the point of self-defeat: 20-63 shouted words per file (ru/09: 54, ru/10: 57, en/09: 63), often 2-3 per paragraph — «между КАЖДОЙ парой фаз», «дренируется ПОЛНОСТЬЮ», "between EVERY pair of phases", "the SET OF AVAILABLE APIs". When everything is capitalised nothing is emphasised, and on a phone the paragraph reads as a rant. It also has a concrete side effect: the mechanical abbreviation checker reports ~100 false positives (EVERY, EACH, ONE, THE, AT, WHAT, ВСЮ, ЗАХОД, КАЖДОЕ), which buries the ~60 real unexpanded acronyms it also found. Bold already exists in these files and is used correctly elsewhere — the fix is to convert emphasis to bold and keep caps only for literal identifiers.
- Every acronym is treated as shared vocabulary. Across all 20 files, not one of GC, CPU, OS/ОС, DNS, TCP, IOCP, JIT, IC, RSS, OOM, TTL, DTO, ORM, TDZ, APM, k8s, cgroup, БД, p99 is expanded at its first use in the file it appears in — GC is used 7x in article 08 and 10x in article 10 without ever being written out once. Only AST and NDJSON get the treatment the whole zone needs (`AST (Abstract Syntax Tree)`), which shows the authors know the pattern and simply did not apply it. Because articles are read out of order and the site has ten of them, 'GC' has to be spelled out ten times.
- The structural habit is strong and worth protecting: almost every section opens with a diagram, a table, or a ❌/✅ code pair, and only then explains. The damage is concentrated in the *closing* paragraph of each such section — a single 40-80-word sentence, hung together with two or three em-dashes, that tries to state the mechanism, the practical consequence, the interview framing, and a cross-reference at once (en/02 81w, ru/02 68w, en/01 56w, ru/08 56w, en/06 57w). These paragraphs are the highest-value target in the zone: splitting each into 3-4 sentences would fix B and F without touching a single technical claim, a diagram, or a code example.
- Articles 04, 09 and 10 open by defining the *shallow* answer before giving the real one — «Поверхностный уровень этой темы — "выучить порядок..."», "The shallow level is 'CommonJS uses require...'" — so the first thing on screen is knowledge the reader is being told not to rely on, and the actual answer arrives 40-60 words later. Articles 01, 05, 07 do the opposite and are the strongest in the zone (07 opens with the failing `readFile` snippet, and its scores are the highest). Where the meta-framing is worth keeping, it belongs after the answer, not in front of it.

**Прочее:** Cross-references (`[The Event Loop]`) are plain bracketed text — there are zero markdown links in all 20 files. This hurts: article 01 spends two 45-56-word sentences listing titles the reader cannot follow, and there is no consistent naming — `[Memory and GC]` (ru/05) vs `[Memory and Garbage Collection]`, `[CommonJS vs ESM]` (01) vs `[CommonJS vs ES Modules]` (10). Article 06 also points to `[WebSockets and Realtime Systems]` and `[Scalability and Load Balancing]`, which are outside this topic.
Factual/consistency slips a reader will notice: both locales of article 10 say "каждый из 45 вопросов выше" / "each of the 45 questions above" but only 33 numbered questions exist; en/06 comments `// modern API, see below` on `os.availableParallelism()` and nothing below discusses it; ru/03 has a Latin 'a' inside «оперaций»; ru/09 has «серверless-функций» mixing scripts; ru/02 has «монографичности» for «мономорфности».
The `<!-- verified: 2026-06-05 -->` marker is present in all 10 ru files and in none of the en files.
RU-specific vocabulary to standardise: «дренируется/дренаж» → «опустошается»; «вулнерабилити» → «уязвимости»; «orchestrator» → «оркестратор» (08 already does this); the apostrophe transliterations «callback'а / chunk'и / instance'ами / trade-off'ами / follow-up'ы / tree-shake'ит» appear in most files and are the single loudest signal of translated-from-English prose.
Nothing in this zone needs its depth cut: the technical content (megamorphic call sites, dual package hazard, external vs heapUsed, dns.lookup pool contention) is the reason the site is worth reading and every worst_place rewrite above preserves it verbatim.

### nodejs-quiz (quiz) — системный рефактор

- Answer-shape bias, same signature as every other bank on the site. correctIndex is 0 in 34/42 and 1 in 8/42 — never 2 or 3. The correct option is the longest in 21/42 outright, and in 21 of the 27 items where the options differ in length at all (the other 15 are event-loop phase lists where all four options are the same length by construction). Because shuffleOptions runs only on the random-quiz route, on the per-topic route the answer is first, every time.
- 40% of the bank is one question asked seventeen times. Items 1, 2, 6, 11, 13, 16, 17, 21, 22, 26, 27, 31, 36, 37, 42, 46, 47 all test event-loop ordering, and several are literally identical: 31, 42 and 47 use the same four lines of code with the same key; 16, 36 and 46 have the same keyed option with a different one-line comment in the stem; 6 and 13 are the same snippet reformatted. The mass duplication is what hides the contradictions — with seventeen tries at the same question, items 2, 11 and 17 ended up keying three different answers to setTimeout-vs-setImmediate, and items 1, 21, 31 and 47 disagree on whether process.nextTick is a phase ("the nextTick phase" in 31 vs "not as a phase itself" in 1). Only 25 distinct concepts are covered by 42 items, and nothing covers http, error-first callbacks, EventEmitter, AsyncLocalStorage, or the module resolution algorithm.
- Explanations reach the right answer and then keep talking themselves out of it. nodejs-quiz-12 states the program hangs and then says chunks would be 1; nodejs-quiz-35's explanation names module B where the key names module A; nodejs-quiz-4 concedes "option C is partially true"; nodejs-quiz-1's explanation refutes its own keyed option. The pattern is a confident first sentence (rubric C is genuinely the bank's strongest axis — nearly every explanation leads with the answer in plain words) followed by two or three sentences of hedging that reintroduce the distractors and, in four cases, endorse them.

**Прочее:** Scores are per locale for the whole bank. No unedited model self-talk and no broken code fences in this bank; all 42 stems parse. Item ids skip 18, 28, 38, 39, 41, 43, 48 (42 items, max id 49). The letter-vs-number split in option references (letters in 3, 4, 5; numbers in 14) suggests two generation passes were merged without a normalising edit. Five stream items use fs.createReadStream without a require of fs (12, 20), which breaks rubric E's self-containment rule for a reader copying the snippet.

### nx (вопросы) — ok

- This bank is the site's best answer-shape template and should be the model in the style guide. Every card is: a heading that is itself the one-line answer ('Target = what to run, executor = how to run it', 'Workspaces manage packages, NX manages tasks', 'Same inputs → replayed result'), then a first sentence that answers directly, then bullets or a numbered pipeline, then a small commented code block, then a pitfall split across 2-3 sentences. Result: 10% of EN sentences over the limit and 2.7% of RU — against 54%/33% in cicd-devops and 52%/36% in bundlers — with no loss of depth (cache hashing, target-config layering, inferred targets and barrel-as-public-API are all covered properly).
- The `**Common pitfall:**` block is still the densest text in the card, even here. 19% of its EN sentences are over the limit versus 6% in the bodies, and the longest sentence in each locale (37w EN / 34w RU, q6) sits inside it. But 0 of 12 blocks are a single sentence, which is exactly what the other two banks get wrong (6/20 in bundlers, 19/20 in cicd-devops). Whatever discipline was applied to pitfalls here is the discipline the other banks need.
- Difficulty seam: not observable — all 12 questions are `junior`, so there is no boundary to break at. Worth noting the inverse: this bank proves the seam is not caused by difficulty. Its junior answers average 169 words (EN) and cover Project Crystal, target-config merge order and cache-hash inputs, i.e. genuinely middle/senior material, at 10% over-limit sentences. Depth and short sentences are not in tension; the other banks' senior tiers just weren't edited.
- The residual RU defect is a thin layer of untranslated or transliterated English on top of otherwise lively Russian, and it concentrates in headings and bullet labels — the highest-visibility, lowest-word-count positions. «composition root» and «скаффолдит» are in `###` headings; «Границы, которые можно принуждать» and «Минимальный buy-in» are in bold bullet labels. The body prose around them is genuinely good («уезжает одним PR», «сползает в запутанный клубок», «CI едет час из-за однострочной правки», «не глядя»).

**Прочее:** Coverage judgement, as asked. 12 questions for a 15-chapter course is not a usable practice surface, and the gap is not uniform: the bank covers chapters 00-04, 07 and parts of 01/08, and covers them well. It has zero questions for chapter 05 (affected — mentioned in six answers, never the subject of one), 06 (libs architecture, tags, module-boundary rules — the enforcement mechanism is named four times and never explained), 09/10/11 (microfrontends, Module Federation in NX, shared-deps pitfalls — three consecutive chapters, nothing), 12 (fullstack Node API), 13 (CI and Nx Cloud — remote caching gets one sentence in q12), 14 (reading an existing workspace). Second, all 12 are `junior`, so a learner who finishes the course has no way to rehearse the material the second half of the course exists to teach; the hardest thing the bank asks is 'what does the cache store'. Concretely: the bank needs ~10-14 more questions, weighted middle/senior, and Module Federation + boundary tags + `affected` in CI are the three highest-value additions. That is a content gap, not a readability one — the 12 questions that exist are the best-written cards I audited, and the verdict `ok` refers to them.

### nx-monorepo (ch 00-07) (курс) — точечные правки

- The English version is systematically harder than the Russian one, and it is a length problem, not a vocabulary problem. RU keeps 3.5-10.5% of sentences over the limit; EN runs 12-26% on the very same chapters (ch00 24%, ch06 25%, ch07 26%). The cause is mechanical: the translator preserved the RU punctuation architecture — semicolon splice, colon, em-dash aside — while adding ~19% more words, so a controlled 38-word RU sentence becomes an uncontrolled 56-word EN one. Fix by splitting at the semicolons and colons that already mark the seams, not by cutting content.
- Every chapter is disciplined about Nx's own vocabulary (target, task, executor, inputs, affected, tags are each defined at first use, in the chapter that owns them) and completely undisciplined about the surrounding industry vocabulary. CI appears 8-15 times per chapter and is never expanded anywhere in the first half; PR, SHA, e2e, AST, squash-merge, codemod, scaffolding, barrel, smart/dumb component, cold start all arrive as if already known. The rule the zone follows implicitly is 'explain what Nx invented, assume what the industry invented' — and the target reader is exactly the person who knows neither.
- The 'Частая ошибка' / 'Common mistake' section is the single densest and longest-sentenced block in all 16 files. It always opens with the same 9-12 line paragraph shape ('Разработчик из single-app мира ...' / 'A developer from the single-app world ...') that packs the wrong reflex, its three consequences and the cure into one breath. It is also the most valuable section in each chapter, which is why it deserves the paragraph break most.
- A small but repeating RU register slip: dev-slang lands mid-sentence where a neutral word was available — «в этом пойнт главы» (ch02), «тикет на выпил» (ch06), «структура репы уехала», «генерить прошлогоднюю структуру» (ch07). Individually charming, collectively they make the text harder for a reader whose Russian technical slang is thinner than the author's.

**Прочее:** Resembles `angular` (targeted-fixes), not `python-fullstack`: both locales are complete, idiomatic and independently authored — there is no Latin/Cyrillic hybrid-word layer here, and the RU reads as native writing, not translation. It falls short of angular's G 4.8 for two reasons only: the slang register above and one genuinely broken sentence in ru/05. Rubric E is the zone's strongest asset (4.9): every chapter opens its exercise with an explicit `Вход: workspace после главы NN`, and every code block carries its file path as the first comment line, so a reader returning after a week can restart from any chapter. Practice coverage is the real gap: the `nx` bank has 12 cards, all `junior`, and mapping them to this range gives ch00 (q1,2,9), ch01 (q3,7), ch02 (q5,11), ch03 (q4,10), ch04 (q8,12), ch07 (q6, dry-run only) — meaning **chapter 05 (affected) and chapter 06 (libs architecture, tags, module boundaries) have zero practice behind them**, and those are the two chapters the course itself calls its core value. The bank also writes `NX` where all 16 chapters write `Nx`. Chapter 06 specifically: judged on the 'assumed rather than taught' risk it holds up well — both axes are stated, tags are shown in project.json, the linter mechanics are traced through the graph, and the `'*' → '*'` placeholder trap is called out explicitly; its only real assumption is the smart/dumb component distinction (worst_places #6).

### nx-monorepo (ch 08-14) (курс) — системный рефактор

- THE dominant pattern: the English version is systematically harder than the Russian one, in every single file of the zone. Over-limit sentences, ru → en: ch08 10.4% → 23.6%; ch09 6.1% → 21.8%; ch10 8.5% → 19.3%; ch11 6.6% → 23.2%; ch12 10.4% → 27.6%; ch13 10.3% → 32.2%; ch14 5.3% → 15.1%. The cause is mechanical and repeatable: Russian joins facts with a dash or a colon and drops the copula, and the translation keeps that single-sentence shape while adding ~19% more words plus English's obligatory articles, auxiliaries and 'that'-clauses. A borderline 28-word RU sentence lands at 40-50 words in EN. Nothing about the technical content needs to change — the fix is a per-file pass that splits every dash-joined RU clause chain into separate EN sentences. Chapter 13 is the worst case (a third of all sentences over limit) and chapters 12 and 11 are close behind.
- Second pattern: acronyms are treated as ambient vocabulary rather than as terms that need a first use. `CI` is used 8-26 times per chapter and is never expanded once in any of the 15 chapters of the course, so the 'explained in the chapter that introduces it' allowance does not apply — it is never introduced at all. The same holds for `MF`, `PR`, `CDN`, `README`, `HMR`, `CORS`, `SSR`, `SEO`, `e2e`. `MF` is worse than merely bare: it is overloaded, meaning «микрофронтенды» in chapters 09 and 14 and 'Module Federation' in chapters 10 and 11 — and in chapter 09 it carries both meanings within a single file. A one-time pass that expands each acronym at its earliest occurrence in the course, plus a decision to write 'Module Federation' in full and reserve MF for microfrontends, fixes all 14 files.
- Third pattern (structural, and mostly a strength worth codifying): every chapter uses the same reliable skeleton — Theory → 'В рабочем монорепо' (five runnable grep/nx commands for someone else's repo) → 'Что добавляем в проект' → exercise with explicit **Вход:** prerequisite → worked solution → Check yourself → Common mistake framed as 'a developer from the single-app world'. Rubric C and E scores are high (4.3 each) precisely because of this skeleton: the **Вход:** line means a reader returning after a week always knows what state the workspace is in, and the 'Common mistake' section reliably names the wrong mental model before correcting it. The one place the skeleton leaks is theory density: the 'Ответы на edge cases' and 'Разбор решения' blocks routinely run 5-16 consecutive paragraphs with no diagram or code between them (ch09 en: 16 paragraphs / 532 words; ch13 en: 8 paragraphs / 495 words; ch12 en: 12 paragraphs / 535 words), which is where the D score of 3.5 comes from.

**Прочее:** Microfrontends overlap: chapters 09-11 COMPLEMENT the `microfrontends` topic rather than duplicate it, with one contradiction to resolve. The topic teaches MF generically and polyrepo-flavoured (hand-written ModuleFederationPlugin configs, iframes, web components, single-spa, style isolation, cross-MFE state, interview answers); the course teaches the same negotiation mechanics strictly through Nx generators and adds material the topic does not have at all — Nx auto-sharing every workspace lib as an unversioned singleton, and the resulting first-wins skew across independently deployed remotes. Overlap is confined to remoteEntry/container, the bootstrap async boundary, singleton/strictVersion/eager, and the two-reacts dispatcher story. Send a reader who wants concepts or interview answers to the topic; send anyone building or auditing a real Nx federation to the course, which is markedly better written (the topic came out systemic-refactor with 40-90-word fact sandwiches). Two things to fix at the seam: the topic frames `strictVersion: true` as a staging/CI-only diagnostic, while course ch11 prescribes it permanently in production for react/router/state libs — pick one; and the two use different abbreviations for the same idea (topic: MFE, expanded once; course: MF, never expanded), with no cross-link in either direction.
Chapter 14 delivers as the practical payoff. It is a real procedure, not a summary: a layer → source-of-truth → what-to-look-for table, seven numbered steps each with a copy-pasteable command, a catalogue of eight archaeological finds with diagnosis and treatment, a 10-question deliverable, a worked reference run against mini-shop, 🔴/🟡/🟢 triage, and an explicit one-fix-per-PR discipline plus a 'don't open the epic cleanup PR' warning. A middle developer could execute it on a real repo in the promised hour or two. Its problems are purely linguistic: CI appears 26 times unexpanded, and the ROI-ordering answer — the single most valuable paragraph in the chapter — is one 74-word (RU) / 85-word (EN) sentence.

### oop-patterns (статьи+вопросы+quiz) — системный рефактор

- THE TEMPLATE MECHANISM HOLDS, AND IT IS NOW A SITE-WIDE RULE. The article template has a bullet slot, a ```txt diagram slot and an ❌/✅ code-pair slot; the bank template has none of the three. Counted across the 8 RU articles: 119 markdown bullets, 39 ```txt diagrams, 81 ❌/✅ markers. Counted across the 34 RU bank answers: 3 bullets (all in one answer), 0 diagrams, 0 ❌/✅ pairs. Every bank answer is the same fixed shape — `### heading` / one-sentence definition / one code fence / one or two undifferentiated prose paragraphs / `**Частая ловушка:**`. With no slot to put a list in, every enumeration collapses into a single sentence. That is the whole 26.2-vs-11.2 gap: long-sentence rate is 0-2% in the RU articles and 42.9% in the RU bank; 3.5-13.1% in the EN articles and 61.3% in the EN bank. The connector differs from `architecture` — there the collapsed list was a semicolon chain, here it is an em-dash + comma + parenthetical chain (prose semicolons are only 2.7x denser in the bank, 4.3 vs 1.6 per 1k, while em-dashes are actually *less* dense than in the articles) — but the cause is identical and the fix is identical: give the bank template a bullet slot and a diagram slot. The clinching evidence is internal: oop-patterns-q-5 is the single answer in the file that uses a bulleted list (the three cloning approaches), and it is by a wide margin the clearest answer in the bank, written by the same author on the same day.
- THE QUIZ IS FIVE QUESTIONS ASKED FIVE TIMES EACH, AND IT TESTS A DIFFERENT LANGUAGE THAN THE ARTICLES. The 25 items cover six distinct ideas: Singleton thread-safety (items 1, 6, 11, 16, 21 — five near-verbatim restatements, three of them with the same Java `getInstance()` snippet), Factory vs Abstract Factory (7, 12, 17, 22), Observer vs Pub/Sub (3, 13, 18, 23), Strategy vs State (4, 9, 14, 19, 24), HOC vs Decorator (5, 10, 15, 20, 25), plus items 2 and 8. Zero items on SOLID, zero on GRASP, zero on Builder, Prototype, Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Facade, Flyweight, Proxy, Command, Iterator, Template Method, Mediator or Chain of Responsibility — i.e. six of the eight articles are untested. Worse, the six Singleton items test JVM shared-memory threading (`synchronized`, `volatile`, reflection and deserialisation attacks, JVM class loading), which the articles never mention and cannot mention: content/topics/oop-patterns/ru/03-creational-patterns.md frames Singleton's three problems as hidden dependency, global mutable state and SRP violation, and content/questions/oop-patterns.json q-8 says «Синглтоны в Node.js — это синглтоны на уровне модуля». A reader who studies the articles will not have been taught anything the Singleton quiz items ask.
- THE BANK'S FIRST SENTENCES ARE THE ZONE'S ONE UNQUALIFIED SUCCESS — AND THE MODEL FOR EVERYTHING ELSE. Rubric C is the bank's best score (4/5, and 0.0% indirect leads mechanically). All 34 answers open with a plain-language one-sentence definition that answers the question asked before any caveat arrives: «Multiton — это Singleton, обобщённый на фиксированный набор именованных инстансов вместо ровно одного», «Facade предоставляет единый упрощённый интерфейс поверх набора подсистем». The failure is that the discipline stops after sentence one. Sentence two routinely runs 60-86 words and stacks three or four new ideas. The style-guide rule to extract: apply the first-sentence discipline to the *second and third* paragraph leads too — every paragraph of a bank answer should open with its own short claim, then support it, rather than opening mid-argument with 'The cost interview answers usually skip:' followed by 62 words.

**Прочее:** D / solid-grasp overlap: `solid-grasp` is a registered topic (src/constants/topics.ts:33, 'SOLID & GRASP') with a 25-question bank and a 25-item quiz but NO content/topics/solid-grasp/ directory at all — its only teaching text is oop-patterns articles 01 (SOLID) and 02 (GRASP), filed under a topic labelled 'OOP Patterns (GoF)'. So this is duplication of scope, not of text, and it runs one way: material is missing from solid-grasp, not repeated. I found no contradictions between the two — article 01's «когда строгое SRP/LSP вредит» sections line up with solid-grasp-q-21/q-23, and article 02's GRASP framing lines up with solid-grasp-q-11..q-20. One real gap: solid-grasp's bank tests Indirection (q-19) and Protected Variations (q-20), two GRASP patterns article 02 never introduces (it covers seven, not nine). Recommendation is editorial, not readability: either point solid-grasp at oop-patterns/01-02 explicitly, or move those two articles. Verdict scope: `systemic-refactor` applies to the four JSON files (bank ru/en, quiz ru/en). The 16 articles are the strongest content I have audited in this project — clean sentences, examples before theory, ❌/✅ pairs everywhere — and need only targeted fixes: expand borrowed acronyms per-file (A is their one weak score, worst in 02 and 08) and fix the `### Анemic Domain Model` heading.

### postgresql (статьи+quiz) — системный рефактор

- Almost all teaching prose lives inside ```txt fenced blocks, not in Markdown. In all 7 articles the Markdown body is one lead paragraph per file (243-719 words total) while every definition, every abbreviation expansion and every trade-off sits inside pre-wrapped monospace blocks. Three consequences for the target reader: (1) the text cannot reflow, so on a phone it is horizontal scrolling or broken wrapping — worst in the 102-char anomaly table in 03, the two-column transaction listing in 03, and the deep-indented EXPLAIN plan tree in 06; (2) abbreviation expansions are typographically demoted to the same weight as code, so "Write-Ahead Log (WAL)" reads as a comment rather than as the definition; (3) the flag script's abbreviation counts are misleadingly low, because expansions inside blocks are invisible to it and unexpanded uses in blocks are too.
- The Russian files are post-edited machine translation with the edit unfinished, and the residue always lands on the explanatory clause. Single English words and whole clauses left inline: «мало enough», «не получит benefit от», «Advantage vs Index Scan: re-sort pages», «Когда: large non-indexed joins», «строится in-memory bitmap (set page numbers)», «помечает space dead tuples как свободный», «статистику по ALL выполненным запросам», «tens of KB vs GBs для B-Tree», «о window функциях здесь». Latin letters inside Russian words: «индекс medленнее». Non-word calques: «ПЕР-ОПЕРАЦИИ»/«ПЕР-СОЕДИНЕНИЮ», «Свежетаблица», «работают корректно с связями» (ties→связи), «из-за природы MVCC только для добавления» (append-only). Plus spaceless em-dashes copied from English typography throughout the quiz («Устаревшая статистика—основная причина»). This is the single highest-value fix in the zone: it is mechanical, it is concentrated in 04, 06, 07 and the quiz, and it currently makes the punchline of several sections unreadable.
- Every RU article H1 is untranslated English («# PostgreSQL Fundamentals», «# Transaction Isolation Levels», «# Indexes and Internals», «# Query Planner и EXPLAIN ANALYZE») while all H2/H3 below it are Russian. The reader lands on an English title in a Russian article, and the cross-links at the bottom of every file («Связь с другими темами») also point at English titles, so the mapping between link and article is a guess.
- Article density is inverted relative to need: 01-06 pace themselves well (a concept, then a runnable example — this is why D and C score highest in the zone at 05 and 03), but 07-postgresql-interview-questions.md, the file a candidate actually rehearses from, is 250 lines with exactly one code block, two flagged theory walls, and 14 unexplained terms in its first two sentences. The interview-questions file needs the opposite treatment from the rest: fewer terms per sentence, and the examples that 01-06 already contain pulled forward.
- The quiz has three structural defects that are independent of wording. (1) In 26 of 29 items the correct option is the longest one (11 RU options exceed 120 characters, the worst at 198) — so the correct answer is guessable by shape, and the long options do not fit a phone line. (2) Four explanations (-26, -27, -29, -30, both locales) refer to answers by letters — "Варианты B, C и D", "Option B describes unique indexes" — but options are stored as an unlabelled array, so the letters point at nothing. (3) Two questions (-22, -25) repeat all four options inline inside the `question` string, so the reader sees them twice. Rubric C is otherwise the zone's strongest: most explanations do state the reason in the first sentence.
- Both the quiz and article 06 lean on SQL the site never teaches. Window functions (ROW_NUMBER, LAG, LEAD, OVER, PARTITION BY) carry 6 of 29 quiz items (-9, -15, -18, -23, -29) and the pg_stat_statements example in 06; JOIN/NULL semantics carry 3 more (-5, -20, -25); CTEs and LATERAL JOIN are name-dropped as selling points in 07. The coverage gap itself is already recorded elsewhere, but the readability consequence is real and fixable without adding an article: those snippets need an inline gloss (one comment line saying what OVER () does, what LAG looks at), because right now the reader is asked to read syntax they were never shown.

**Прочее:** Four factual conflicts surfaced while auditing and will read as comprehension failures: quiz-17 asserts "REPEATABLE READ может допустить фантомные чтения" while article 03 states twice that PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ does prevent them; quiz-10 expands SSI as "Serialization Anomaly Detection" while quiz-17 and article 03 give the correct "Serializable Snapshot Isolation"; quiz-16 makes "stale statistics" a distractor for a question nearly identical to quiz-1 and quiz-11, where it is the correct answer. Not scored as readability, but they undo the articles.
RU 01 lines 155-158 show a CREATE TABLE with three mutually exclusive ON DELETE clauses joined by commas — not valid SQL; the EN file fixed this by commenting two of them out. RU also has "ORDERED BY" for "ORDER BY" in 06.
Quiz redundancy: 29 items cover roughly 8 concepts — VACUUM is asked 4 times (-4, -8, -14, -19), "which index for range queries" 4 times (-3, -7, -13, -21), MVCC's benefit twice (-22, -26). Not a readability defect, but it means the abbreviation and option-length problems repeat with no new content.
Articles 05 and 03 are the models to copy: MVCC expanded at first use in the lead paragraph, one concept per example, zero over-length sentences in RU 05.
I did not open content/questions/postgresql.json, per the task.

### prisma (статьи+вопросы) — системный рефактор

- THE DOMINANT PATTERN — the bank is 14 topics wearing 40 hats, and the thin copy contradicts the good one. Every subject appears 2-4 times: schema (q-1/21), CRUD (q-2/22/25), one-to-many (q-3/23), migrations (q-4/24), client+pooling (q-5/16/35/40), nested writes (q-6/26/31), select-vs-include (q-7/27), pagination (q-8/15/28/32), raw SQL (q-11/29), middleware (q-13/30), generators (q-17/36), multi-schema (q-18/38), Prisma-vs-TypeORM (q-19/37), N+1 (q-14/34/39). In each pair one answer is written properly (a real mechanism, version caveats, numbers) and the other is a 40-90-word restatement whose pitfall is a generic one-liner. Because nobody reconciled them, the pairs now teach different things: q-7 vs q-27 on whether include/select can nest, q-16 vs q-35 vs q-40 on where connection_limit lives, q-17 vs q-36 on whether `@prisma/internals` or `@prisma/generator-helper` is the generator API (q-36 explicitly names q-17's choice as the trap). Deduplicating is the single highest-value fix in this zone and it removes nothing: every thin answer's content is already inside its fuller twin.
- Difficulty labels do not track depth. Five answers tagged `senior` (q-34, q-35, q-38, q-39, q-40) are 55-90 prose words and answerable by a junior, while the articles cover the same ground far deeper: q-34/q-39 give N+1 = 'use include or select', where ru/05 gives diagnosis via `log: ['query']` plus three graded solutions plus the Cartesian-product counter-warning; q-35/q-40 give pooling = 'use a singleton', where ru/05 gives `connection_limit`, `pool_timeout`, the serverless `connection_limit=1` rule and PgBouncer/Accelerate. The bank's low mechanical flag density is exactly this: those answers are too short to contain a long sentence.
- Articles put a code or txt block under every new idea — and article 07 is the same content with the blocks removed. Files 01-06 score D 4-5 because the habit is rigorous: claim, then snippet with inline comments, then the next claim. File 07 (both locales) has one code block for 18 answers and a 35-paragraph run, and it is the only genuinely hard-to-read file in the zone. The repair is mechanical: 07's answers and 01-06's snippets are already about the same things.
- Latin-script terms are used as running Russian words and never glossed once: «schema-first подход», «runtime-ошибка», «Nested Writes», «Referential Actions», «source of truth», «workaround», «locality», «page splits», «overhead», «inference», «seq scan», «eager loading». All six RU article H1s are untranslated English («# Prisma Fundamentals», «# Prisma Schema and Models», …), as are many section heads («## CI/CD pipeline с Prisma», «## Bulk операции»). This is the main driver of G = 2.9 in files that are otherwise written in living Russian.
- The RU bank's thin tier is visibly unedited machine translation, and the tells are mechanical enough to grep: hyphen used as a dash (« - » in q-5, 7, 11, 13, 28, 33), em dash with no surrounding spaces carried over from English (10 RU / 12 EN answers), an English preposition left in place («per запрос», q-16), nominalised calques of English gerunds («Не ожидание `next(params)`», q-30), and a bare grammar error («Создание новый экземпляра», q-5). None of these appear in the ten well-written answers, so the fix is scoped to a known list.

**Прочее:** Two premises in the brief are false positives worth correcting upstream. (1) The pitfall marker is present in 40/40 answers, not 0/40 — it is just labelled «Типичная ошибка на интервью» (25) / «Типичная ошибка» (15) and "Common interview trap" (40), so an exact-string search for "Common pitfall / Частая ловушка" finds nothing. (2) The 73/78-word average is prose-only; including code the answers average 135 RU / 139 EN words. The thinness verdict still stands, but it is a two-tier bank (~10 substantial answers, ~15 thin, ~15 middling), not a uniformly short one. Beyond readability: ru/02 and en/02 declare three `@id` fields in one `model Product`, which Prisma rejects; ru/03 and en/03 declare `model User` and `model Post` twice inside one block; ru/02 labels a BRIN index as full-text search with invalid `type: BrinIndex` syntax (EN dropped this line, so RU is the outlier); bank q-24 says `migrate deploy` applies "uncommitted"/«незакоммиченные» files where it means unapplied; bank q-15 calls `skip` the cursor position.

### python (вопросы) — системный рефактор

- THE dominant defect: every one of the 98 answers ends with a **Common pitfall / Частая ловушка** paragraph, and that paragraph is a single sentence in 89/98 EN and 88/98 RU answers. Median length 60 words (EN) / 53 words (RU), max 103 / 96. The template is always the same: a gerund naming the mistake, an em-dash, then two or three consequences chained with 'since / so that / because', plus one or two parentheticals. 96/98 EN and 94/98 RU of these opening sentences exceed the word limit, and 98/98 answers contain at least one over-limit sentence — so the bank's over-limit count is not driven by scattered long sentences but by one writing habit applied 98 times. Fix: keep every claim, split into 3-4 sentences, and put the actionable advice first rather than last.
- Rubric C fails in two distinct ways, both structural. (a) **Problem-first leads** (~14 answers: q5, q13, q35, q38, q42, q44, q48, q55, q78, q90, q92, q93, q94, q97): the opening sentence describes the pain, the 'before' state, or the thing that was *not* asked about, and the subject of the question arrives in sentence two or paragraph two. q55 is the clearest — the question is about `__slots__` and the 63-word lead is about `__dict__`. (b) **Overloaded leads** (~25 more answers, e.g. q28, q32, q37, q39, q40, q50, q52, q54, q57): the lead does land the answer, but it also swallows the mechanism, the contrast and the error class into one 35-60 word sentence, so the caveats sit *inside* the essence instead of after it. The pyramid is intact in intent and broken in punctuation.
- 17 dead cross-references per locale ('covered in a related question' ×11, 'covered in a separate question' ×2, 'as covered' ×4; RU «в связанном вопросе» ×11 plus «разбиралось/разбирался» ×14). Question-bank cards are read in shuffled order and carry no links, so these are unfollowable pointers that also imply something was withheld. Either inline the one clause the reader needs (as in the q60 rewrite above) or drop the reference.
- The densest paragraph of every answer is the last one and has no example, diagram or code under it — the pitfall closer always comes after the final code block. This is why theory_walls is 0 while long_paragraphs is 124 (RU) / 99 (EN): the walls are single paragraphs, not runs. Breaking the closer into short sentences fixes both the B and D symptom at once.

**Прочее:** Difficulty seam: YES, and it starts one tier earlier than in `typescript`. Over-limit sentence rate RU 31%(junior) -> 54%(middle) -> 62%(senior) -> 79%(advanced); EN 48% -> 74% -> 74% -> 88%. Words per sentence RU 24.7 -> 33.2 -> 34.6 -> 43.2. Indirect leads RU 6% -> 40% -> 67% -> 45%, EN 11% -> 50% -> 70% -> 55%. So it is a monotonic gradient with the sharpest single step at junior->middle (over-limit rate roughly doubles, indirect leads jump 6x), peaking in `advanced` for syntax and in `senior` for leads. The 18 junior answers are genuinely clean and can be used as the style reference for fixing the rest.
EN is harder than RU here, unusually so: EN uses 10% MORE words (20725 vs 18764) for the same content and blows a TIGHTER limit (25 vs 28) at 71% vs 56%. Above-B2 vocabulary and idiom: 'closure gymnastics', 'sharp edges', 'trips people up', 'slip past casual code review', 'earns its place', 'hoisted out', 'funneling all bytecode execution', 'de-optimizes', 'orthogonal concerns', 'conflating', 'referent', 'arity', 'biased/deferred reference counting'. Stacked modifiers are pervasive ('a lightweight, cooperatively-scheduled pseudo-thread', 'an opt-in, experimental build'). 'Reaching for X' is used as a stock opener 9 times.
What is genuinely good and must not be touched: senior-level depth (metaclass conflicts, greenlet bridge, PEP 659/703/554, variance, cell objects) with zero dumbing down; code examples are the best of any bank measured — self-contained, output shown inline as comments, narrow-screen-friendly, commented exactly at the non-obvious line; JS/TS bridges (jest.fn, beforeEach/beforeAll, V8, NumPy views) are placed well for the target audience; RU is living language, not calque (osushchestvlyaetsya 0, «в случае если» 0, «данный» only 2 real hits, no genitive noun-stacking).
Two non-readability defects found while reading, reported for completeness: python-q-88 EN cites `.finalize_obj()`, which does not exist (see worst_places); python-q-69 EN has an unbalanced parenthesis — '("does it explicitly declare itself as this type?", which is how ordinary class inheritance and `isinstance` checks normally work.' — the RU version closes it correctly.
Verdict rationale: the content needs no rewrite, but 98/98 answers carry an over-limit sentence and 96/98 carry an over-limit pitfall opener, so the language pass covers the whole zone — that is `systemic-refactor` by the rubric's definition, even though the fix is narrow and mechanical (split the closer, unpack the lead).

### python-fullstack (ch 00-09) (курс) — системный рефактор

- The RU version is a translation of the EN version, and the translation leaks in six places across five chapters — «nothing works» and «historically argparse позволял» (ch 00), «compiler вынужден определять» (ch 03), «где curates публичный API» (ch 05), «С relatively недавним предложением» (ch 06), «machinально» and «баг molчит» (ch 08). Each sits at exactly the position its English counterpart occupies in the EN file, and two of them are broken mid-word (Latin stem + Cyrillic suffix). Three markup typos cluster with them: a misplaced closing quote in ru/06 (`примитив "поверх" \`try/finally",`), a stray pipe in ru/08 (`` `path.open()|) ``), and a lost agreement in ru/05 («дефолтная автообнаружение … рассчитано»). This is not a style problem — it is a QA gap, and it is the fastest fix with the highest payoff in the zone.
- Language complexity drifts monotonically upward as the chapters get harder, in both locales — the same drift the `python` question bank showed at the junior→middle boundary, but smooth rather than a sharp seam. Long sentences: RU 17%→34% (ch 01→09), EN 24%→46% (ch 01→07). Over-long paragraphs: RU 2→9, EN 2→9. The break point is chapter 03-04, where EN crosses 39% and never comes back; RU crosses 26% at ch 04 and never comes back. Chapters 00-02 read cleanly for the target reader; chapters 05, 08 and 09 do not. The content did not get harder proportionally — the sentences did, because each new fact was appended to the existing sentence with an em-dash instead of starting a new one.
- Zero diagrams and one table across all 20 files. The site has a diagram convention and this course uses none of it, which is why the flag script counts 52 theory walls. The most defensible cost is chapter 05, the most abstract chapter in the zone: it argues at length that «относительные импорты считают уровни пакетной иерархии, а не буквальные шаги по файловой системе» — a claim about two trees that differ — and never draws either tree. The second cost is structural: every chapter's «Частая ошибка» section is two 10-to-16-line prose paragraphs with no code at all, sitting at the end of a chapter that has otherwise taught the reader entirely through runnable examples.
- The JS bridge is the course's strongest and most consistent asset and must not be touched. Every chapter opens each theory block by naming the JS reflex that will mislead the reader, and every chapter closes theory with an explicit «Параллели с JS/TS/Node» list. Rubric C is a flat 4.0 across all 20 files because of this: bolded term, then the point, then the caveats. The «Ключевые решения» bullets after each worked solution do the same job for code. Nothing in the refactor should change section structure — only sentence length inside it.

**Прочее:** Course-format adjustments applied as instructed; they moved A and E up, not down. On A: LEGB (ch 03), ABC (ch 04) and AST (ch 09) are expanded inline and are false positives from the script — the real misses are CLI (used 10x in the ch 00 title and never spelled out anywhere in the course), REPL, TC39 and PEP. On E: chapters 06, 07 and 09 explicitly state which files are unchanged since the previous chapter, which is exactly what the course rubric asks for — but they then print only the changed files, so the full project state exists nowhere after chapter 05, and a reader returning after a week to ch 07 must reconstruct `cli/parser.py` and `cli/app.py` from two chapters back. Three theory snippets are also not self-contained: ch 06's `FileLock` uses `fcntl` with no `import fcntl`, ch 07's `partial` example uses `sys.stderr` with no `import sys`, ch 08's `db_connection` references an undefined `DB_PATH`. One term genuinely appears before the chapter that owns it: SQL, first used in ch 07 (`itertools.groupby` vs "SQL GROUP BY"), introduced in ch 08.

### python-fullstack (ch 10-18) (курс) — системный рефактор

- Untranslated or half-translated English leaks into the Russian text in five of the nine RU chapters, and in three of them the word is a Latin/Cyrillic hybrid that cannot be read at all: 'materializироваться' and 'materializируется' (18, twice in one sentence), 'транзitively' (17), plus whole English words dropped into Russian sentences — '— but сама функция' and '"as any hidden"' (10), '# ДО исправления — was в storage/...' (13), 'станет action неудобным' (12), 'которая resolves перед роутом' / 'resolving перед ним' (14). Add to that the English possessive 's grafted onto Russian ('log_command's wrapper', "Docker's HEALTHCHECK", "Node's Worker Threads") and one dropped space ('даётту же самую пользу', 15). These are not style choices; they read as an unfinished translation pass and they cluster in the two chapters a reader is most likely to skim (17-18).
- The English version is systematically harder than the Russian, and the gap widens exactly where the material gets harder. Over-limit sentences: ch10 26%->41%, ch11 29%->51%, ch12 34%->50%, ch13 35%->47%, ch14 35%->47%, ch16 35%->51%. The cause is not extra content — it is that the RU sentence was already at the limit and the ~19% English expansion pushes it over, compounded by an idiom habit the RU does not have: 'earns its keep', 'pays for itself', 'the box is already checked', 'only half the journey', 'a dead end on both sides', 'nowhere to come from', 'a one-time box to tick', 'beefier version', 'gets in the way'. A B1-B2 reader on a phone loses one of these per paragraph.
- Every chapter opens its theory sections correctly — a bolded lead sentence that states the point in plain words, then the caveats — but the caveat then gets stuffed back into the lead sentence as a parenthesis. The GIL definition (ch11) puts 40 words of caveats between subject and verb; the same shape recurs in ch13's Pydantic coercion note and ch14's exception-handler typing note. The fix is mechanical and does not lose a single fact: lead sentence, full stop, caveats as the next paragraph.
- The difficulty ramp is supported everywhere except the last chapter. Chapters 10-17 each introduce one idea, show it in runnable code, and often show the real terminal output or the real mypy error it produced (ch11's three timed experiments and ch13's blank-text transaction bug are the strongest examples on the site). Chapter 18 breaks the pattern: it is 3155 words with zero code, 14 long paragraphs, and roughly fifteen tools and concepts named but never shown (SIGTERM, readiness vs liveness, grace period, token bucket, sliding window, contextvars, Alembic, asyncpg, Celery, RabbitMQ, slowapi, Fluentd/Vector/Promtail, Loki/ELK/CloudWatch). It is the one place in the range where the chapter assumes more than it teaches.
- Course-wide terminology gaps that my chapters inherit rather than cause: CLI is used ~30 times across the whole course and expanded nowhere, in either language; SQL first appears in ch07 and is never expanded; ASGI, ORM, DTO, REST, TCP, ELK, RAM and CPU appear for the first time in chapters 13-18 and are expanded nowhere. Since a course is read in order, the fix is one expansion at the true first use (CLI in ch00, SQL in ch07, ASGI in ch14, DTO/REST in ch13, ORM in ch14, the rest in ch18).

**Прочее:** Two content defects found while auditing, reported for the owner rather than as readability findings: (1) ch15's exercise says create storage/users_storage.py but its worked solution imports `from ..storage import users as users_storage`, and ch16 imports `users_storage` — chapter 15's solution as printed will not import; (2) ch15 never shows the models/__init__.py and auth/__init__.py re-exports that its own imports depend on. Chapter 11 scores highest on D and E in the whole range (three experiments with real measured numbers) and lowest on F — its problem is purely sentence length in the EN version, not structure. Verdict is systemic-refactor rather than targeted-fixes only because of language: structure (C/D/E) is sound and should not be touched.

### rabbitmq (статьи) — точечные правки

- Abbreviations are expanded once per ZONE, not once per FILE, and the expansion always lives in the earliest article that mentions the term. AMQP is spelled out in 01 and 02 but bare in 03; TTL and DLQ are spelled out in 03 and then used bare in 04, 05, 06 and 07 — including in 04, whose whole subject is dead-lettering. 'Visibility timeout' and 'redrive policy' are explained only in 05 and used bare in 07. QoS, TPS, SNS, HA, SLA and FIFO are never expanded anywhere in the zone. Since files are read out of order, the deepest articles are the least self-contained.
- Article 07 abandons the format that makes 01-06 work. Articles 01-06 back every new concept with a code block, an ASCII diagram or a bullet list within a paragraph or two. Article 07 is 2.2-2.6k words with zero diagrams and zero code blocks, and every enumeration that would be a bullet list in 01-06 is inlined as '(1) … (2) … (3) …' inside a single 45-64 word sentence. This is the zone's only self-test surface (no question bank, no quiz), so the format costs the most exactly where the reader is meant to be recalling rather than reading.
- The English version is consistently harder than the Russian for the same content. Russian files have 0-1 sentences over the length threshold each; English files have 3-26 (07: 15.1% of all sentences). English also adds idiom the Russian renders plainly: 'this works fine until it doesn't', 'it falls over entirely', 'gets hammered with', 'the most important tuning knob', 'pays for itself', 'poison pill', 'the scaling story', 'blind-retry'. Three EN-only defects have no ru counterpart at all: the 'goroutines' leak (03), the broken quote markup (03), and the garbled saga diagram (06).
- Russian keeps English terms as bare loanwords with no gloss on first use in the file: downstream, replay, retention, payload, backoff, upsert, rate limit, fan-out, eventual consistency, best practice, батчинг. Most are genuinely untranslatable in this domain, but the first occurrence in each file needs three words of Russian in brackets — the articles already do this well for offset, wire-level, wildcards and quorum queues, so the habit exists and is just applied unevenly.

**Прочее:** 01 stands on its own and does not contradict kafka/01 or system-design/05 — it is RabbitMQ-flavoured (durable vs persistent, DB-as-queue, push/pull, publisher confirms) where sd/05 is broker-agnostic (queue/pubsub/streaming table, Prisma idempotency) and kafka/01 motivates the log. It genuinely repeats delivery guarantees, DLQ and idempotency, told a third time with different examples.
05 and kafka/06 agree on every substantive claim (log vs queue, push vs pull, replay, routing, native DLX, no Kafka priority, 'Kafka is not automatically better'). Two frictions: 05 says '~50k–150k msg/sec per node', kafka/06 says 'hundreds of thousands per second'; and kafka/06 says a RabbitMQ consumer 'has no direct control over receive rate' while rabbitmq/01 and 03 present prefetch as exactly that control.
A real cross-zone contradiction: kafka/01 and kafka/06 both claim that adding a consumer on RabbitMQ 'requires changes to Order Service', while rabbitmq/02 and 06 state (correctly) that a new queue bound to a fanout/topic exchange needs zero producer changes. Kafka's framing should be fixed, not RabbitMQ's.
Internal contradiction inside this zone: 04 argues exactly-once is not achievable at broker level, while 05 lists SQS FIFO as 'Delivery: exactly-once (deduplication ID prevents duplicates)' with no caveat.
One technical inconsistency inside 05 (both locales): SQS FIFO throughput is '~3k TPS' in the summary block and '300 TPS (or 3,000 with batching)' 40 lines later.

### react (вопросы) — системный рефактор

- THE dominant pattern: the pyramid is present but its apex is a paragraph. In ~30 answers the first sentence really is the direct answer — and then packs the definition, the mechanism and the caveat into one dash-chained clause chain of 35-55 words in RU and 45-118 words in EN (q-7, q-10, q-17, q-19, q-37, q-39, q-48, q-71, q-74, q-78, q-82, q-83, q-98). The fix is never to cut a fact: it is to split the apex into 2-4 sentences that carry the same 3-4 facts. This one habit accounts for most of the 761 over-long-sentence flags and for the majority of the 75 'indirect lead' flags, which are not actually indirect — just too long to land.
- 11 of 98 answers (q-5, q-30, q-33, q-43, q-45, q-46, q-47, q-49, q-87, q-88, q-89) open directly with a 15-30 line code fence and no prose lead at all. For a phone reader in a short burst this is a full screen of scrolling before any statement of the answer. Every one of these already contains a perfectly good lead sentence — it is just sitting below the code, where it reads as commentary instead of as the answer.
- Explanatory paragraphs are almost always introduced by a bold label («**Почему обычное `=` не работает:**», '**The trade-off:**', '**Что НЕ перехватывается:**'). This is a genuinely good, scannable habit and should be kept. But the label is then followed by a single 60-130-word sentence, so the scannability stops at the colon: the reader can find the paragraph they want and then still cannot read it in one pass. Labels should introduce 2-4 short sentences, not one long one.
- The senior tier (q-51 through q-68) is written in a visibly different and much better register than the rest of the bank: `###` sub-headings instead of bold labels, short declarative sentences, plain hyphens, and 'Типичная ошибка на интервью' / 'Common interview trap' as the closing section. It is the most readable third of the zone at the highest difficulty level, which proves the depth is not what makes the other tiers hard. That register is the model the junior/middle/advanced tiers should be brought toward.
- RU carries a recurring layer of English grammar left untranslated: «запрос в полёте» (in-flight request, 5 entries), «опаковый ID» (opaque), «рябь ре-рендеров» (ripple of re-renders), «не гоняющаяся сама с собой» (doesn't race itself), «гейтить», «репервизация», «неоформленные примитивы» (unstyled primitives), «нет хука для закрытия» (no hook for tearing down — where «хук» already means a React hook two lines earlier). Individually minor, collectively they make the RU read as a translation rather than as Russian.
- Abbreviation discipline is the weakest single axis. UI is used 21-25 times and never expanded anywhere in either locale. DOM is expanded exactly once, in q-14, while 28 other uses are spread across answers a reader may open first (q-1, q-2, q-6, q-20, q-28, q-51, q-66, q-98). q-97 alone introduces ICU, CLDR, LTR, RTL and i18n and expands none of the five. Because a question bank is read out of order, 'it is expanded in another answer' does not help — each answer needs its own first-use gloss.

**Прочее:** The script's '17 answers lack the pitfall marker' is a false positive: the whole senior tier (q-51..q-68, 18 answers) closes with «Типичная ошибка на интервью» / 'Common interview trap' instead. All 98 answers in both locales do have a closing pitfall section — the convention is consistent per tier, not missing.
Six answers contain no code block at all (q-48, q-51, q-66, q-71, q-79, q-94) and these are exactly the theory walls the script flagged; each would carry an existing-style diagram or table well — q-51 a two-tree/alternate diagram, q-58 already has an inline timeline that q-71 and q-94 could copy.
95 code lines exceed 95 characters across 53 answers (worst: q-77, q-76, q-98, q-91, q-96, q-50, q-44) — this is the only real threat to the otherwise strong E score, and it is a pure line-wrapping fix with no change to behaviour.
One technical staleness note outside the rubric: q-84 builds its Tabs on `React.cloneElement` without flagging that it is deprecated in React 19, while q-59 does correctly note the React 19 ref changes.
If the two locales were scored separately for verdict, `ru` would be targeted-fixes; `en` alone forces systemic-refactor, because 511 of its 886 sentences are over the limit and the fix is a sentence-splitting pass over every entry.

### react (статьи) — системный рефактор

- The Russian is a translation, not Russian writing, and it leaks in four recurring shapes: (1) English nouns declined with an apostrophe — «server component'ов», «Client'ом», «MouseTracker'ом», «Profiler'а», «fallback'ом», «date-picker'ов», «Provider'ы», «callback'а»; (2) bare English words used as Russian words mid-sentence — «нет mismatch», «memo'd», «до resolve», «in-flight Promise», «timing мог вызывать мерцание»; (3) invented transliterated verbs and nouns — «суспендит», «стримится», «Колокация»/«Коллоцировать», «стейтовая логика», «слайс», «битмаск-система»; (4) word-for-word calques that lose the meaning — «в полёте», «запрос в полёте», «CSS-содержание» (containment→contents, actively wrong), «Поресурсный» (route-based→nonsense), «Водопадов нет», «оставляя работу голодать», «изобретение колеса, плохо». Three of these — «в полёте», «опаковый»-style bare English nouns, and the invented verbs — are the identical defects already flagged in the react question bank, so this is a topic-wide translation habit and not a per-file slip.
- The abbreviation habit from the question bank is reproduced exactly: DOM appears 90 times per locale across the 22 files and is expanded zero times; UI appears 17 times per locale and is expanded zero times. Add JSX, RSC, SSG, TTFB, SWR, SWC, CPU, ARIA, XSS, HOC — all used raw. Because articles are read out of order this bites hardest in file 11 (11 unexpanded acronyms in one file) and file 07 (DOM, SSG, TTFB plus «wire format», «shell», «payload», «server-only»).
- Files 01-10 follow a good, consistent shape — lead sentence answers first, then a code block or ASCII diagram per idea, then a 'Типичные ловушки на интервью' block. File 11 breaks that shape completely: 3.6k RU / 4.4k EN words, 128 paragraphs, zero code blocks, zero diagrams, zero tables, every answer a single 60-100 word prose slab, and its own divergent Russian terminology («согласователь» for reconciler, «нарезка времени» for Time slicing, «лейаут» for layout, «слайс» for срез). It reads as if written by a different author from the ten articles that precede it, and it is the file a job-hunting reader will open last and trust most.
- The Russian register switches hard mid-zone with no mixing inside any file: articles 01-07 address the reader as «вы» (8/8/2/5/2/6/3 hits, zero «ты»), articles 08-11 as «ты» (9/5/3/28 hits, zero «вы»). A reader moving from 07 to 08 is suddenly on informal terms with the text.
- The English is consistently harder than the Russian, and the gap is widest exactly where sentences are longest: en/11 has 53 long sentences (19.6 % of all sentences, longest 67 words) against ru/11's 14 (5.2 %); en/10 has 10 (10.9 %) against ru/10's 3. The pattern is that a 'Common interview traps' answer is written as one paragraph of three or four sentences each carrying three or four facts, and the ~19 % word inflation of English pushes every borderline RU sentence over the limit.

**Прочее:** C (4.1) and E (4.4) are the zone's real strengths — leads answer first and code examples are self-contained, runnable and free of cross-example dependencies. Do not touch them. Three ASCII diagrams have broken box alignment and will wrap badly on a phone: the 'What runs where' two-column table in 07 (76 chars, and the EN version's `Run:` rows do not line up between columns), the flame-chart boxes in 08, and the linked-list traversal in 05 (Nav's sibling is drawn indented under Nav). Two content-level translation errors are worth a separate ticket, not just a language pass: «Поресурсный code splitting» (ru/08) and «CSS-содержание» (ru/09 twice, ru/11 once). One outright typo: «депроритизации» in ru/11 (should be «деприоритизации»); one gender-agreement error: «React Compiler (ранее называлась...)» in ru/10.

### react-quiz (quiz) — системный рефактор

- Answer-shape bias makes the whole bank guessable without reading the question. correctIndex is 0 in 34/44 and 1 in 10/44 — never 2 or 3 — and the correct option is the longest one in 31/44. Because shuffleOptions is applied only on the random-quiz route, on the per-topic route the reader sees the correct answer first and longest, every single time. Two of the three tell-tales are in the data itself: the correct option is the only one that carries a second clause ("...enabling correct state persistence", "...while an uncontrolled component manages its own value via the DOM"), and the distractors are one-liners.
- The bank is six restated questions, not 44. Ten items ask what the key prop is for (2, 8, 13, 17, 22, 24, 27, 33, 37, 47), eight ask useMemo vs useCallback (4, 15, 20, 25, 35, 40, 45, 49), ten log render/effect order (3, 7, 10, 12, 16, 26, 32, 38, 42, 46), five ask controlled vs uncontrolled (5, 14, 19, 34, 48), four ask the Rules of Hooks (1, 11, 41, 18) — 37 of 44 items. Inside those clusters items 1/11/41 are the same code with a renamed condition, 42/46 the same code with one extra console.log, and 12/16/26 the same counter. The restatements are also where the contradictions come from: with ten near-identical key-prop items, nobody noticed that 17 keys the opposite of 13, 27 and 47. Nothing in the bank covers refs, portals, error boundaries, useLayoutEffect, transitions, custom hooks or Server Components.
- Explanations argue against option numbers instead of against ideas. react-quiz-18, -48 and -49 name «option 1»/«Вариант 4» etc.; thirteen more say «The other options misunderstand...» without saying which claim is wrong or why. Both forms fail on the random-quiz route (positions are permuted), and the second form gives the reader nothing to learn from — the distractor's error is the most teachable part of a quiz item and it is systematically left unstated.

**Прочее:** Scores are per locale for the whole bank; item-level detail is in mechanical_counts and worst_places. One rendering artifact: react-quiz-38's stem opens with a bare `jsx` line and no ``` fence, so the code renders as prose in both locales. react-quiz-50 uses ThemeContext without defining it, breaking E's self-containment rule. Item ids skip 21, 30, 36, 39, 43, 44 (44 items, max id 50) — deleted items were not renumbered, which matters if explanations are ever keyed to ids. No unedited model self-talk found in this bank (unlike quiz/css-html), and no item lacks a correct option.

### redis (статьи) — системный рефактор

- Six of the seven articles are heading → code fence with nothing in between. Across articles 01-06 the total prose is ~250 words per file, and most of it is the closing 'Типичные ошибки' bullets; the explanation of what a thing is and when to reach for it lives inside code comments. 03-caching-patterns has no explanatory sentence at all. The fix is not more content — it is one lead sentence per H2, answering 'what is this and when do I use it' before the fence opens.
- Article 07 then fails in the exact opposite direction: 1834 (RU) / 2054 (EN) words of dense prose with two code blocks and four theory walls of 280-700 words. The zone has no single file with a normal prose/code rhythm — the reader swings from all-code to all-prose. The diagrams that would break 07 up already exist in articles 04-06 and could be reused verbatim.
- Abbreviations are introduced in headings and never expanded anywhere in the topic. TTL is used 30+ times in both locales and never once spelled out; the same for HA and SPOF. RDB and AOF are expanded in 06 but used 18 times in 07 without expansion, and 07 is the revision file. Zone-wide A average is 1.9 — the lowest score in this report by a wide margin.
- The RU files read as English scaffolding with Russian connective tissue. Five of seven RU H1 titles are pure English ('Redis Fundamentals', 'Redis Data Structures', 'Redis Caching Patterns', 'Distributed Locks', 'Redis Persistence'); section headings switch script mid-phrase ('Проблема Race Condition в distributed системах', 'Session Storage паттерн'); and the topic's opening definition puts 'in-memory data store' next to its own Russian translation.
- Numbers drift between files with no cross-reference: HyperLogLog error is ~0.81% in 02 and ~1.5% in 07; Streams throughput is ~100k-500k/sec in 04 and ~100k/sec in 07; 01 gives Redis latency as ~100μs while 07 gives memory read as ~100ns with no note that these measure different things. A reader revising from 07 will state numbers the articles contradict.

**Прочее:** Caching overlap: http-rest/03 and web-performance/07 cover the HTTP layer (Cache-Control, ETag, CDN, Service Worker) — a different layer, no conflict with this topic. system-design/03-caching covers exactly the same server-side ground as redis/03 (Cache-Aside, Write-Through/Behind, eviction, stampede, invalidation) and I found no factual contradiction between them — the stampede fixes are complementary, not competing. But system-design/03 opens each idea with prose ('Зачем нужен кеш — снятие нагрузки, а не "ускорение"') and redis/03 is the same content with the explanation removed, so redis/03 does not stand alone: it reads as an appendix. Borrowing system-design/03's framing sentences would fix the worst C score in this zone at no cost to depth.

### rxjs (статьи) — точечные правки

- The English version is systematically harder than the Russian one, and by far more than the usual ~19% expansion. Over-limit sentences: en/04 14.4% vs ru/04 1.1%; en/06 16.0% vs ru/06 6.2%; en/08 22.6% vs ru/08 7.4%; en/01 14.9% vs ru/01 2.7%. The cause is visible sentence by sentence: where the Russian splits a rule into two short sentences or a bullet, the English joins them with a semicolon or an em-dash and adds a parenthetical. On top of that the English reaches for idiom where the Russian is plain — "the tell", "a downed service", "finish it off", "in promise-land", "the crux", "stumps you", "a straight-up bug", "unrolls anything iterable", "waits out the window", "picks up the destruction context". Every one of these has a plain B1-B2 equivalent and the Russian already uses it. F is the lowest-scoring criterion in the zone (2.9) while G is the highest (4.3).
- Every article carries exactly one wide box-drawing decision table (99-123 characters), and in three articles that table is the FIRST thing under its heading, before any prose defines the thing being tabulated (ru/02 «Откуда берутся потоки», ru/07 «share и shareReplay», ru/06 «finalize» — where the table actually summarises all eight error operators, not finalize). The marble diagrams themselves are fine at 65-85 characters and their annotation lines, not the marbles, drive that width; the box tables are the mobile problem. Fix is mechanical and does not touch content: move the lead sentence above the table, and split the widest column out into a list under the diagram.

**Прочее:** Marble-diagram verdict: the notation is taught properly (art. 03 «Как читать marble-диаграмму»), and every diagram before it carries its own inline legend, so nothing is assumed — but the formal lesson sits in file 3 of 8 while files 1 and 2 already use the notation. Coverage is uneven: the four flattening operators (04) and combineLatest/withLatestFrom/forkJoin/zip (05) get first-class diagrams, while merge, concat, race, startWith (05), scan vs reduce (03), take/distinctUntilChanged (03), timeout and finalize (06) and takeUntil ordering (07) get prose only — and `concat`'s infinite-first-source trap in particular would be self-evident on one marble line. Article 08 has zero diagrams across 79 paragraphs. On the operator-choice question the zone is genuinely strong: 04 gives a three-question selection algorithm plus a "cost of getting it wrong" column, 05 opens with three questions, 03 ends every time-operator with a plain-words criterion — this is the best-executed part of the zone and should be the model for other topics. Widths measured: box tables ru 104-118 / en 99-123 chars; marble diagrams ru 65-84 / en 68-85.

### security (статьи+вопросы+quiz) — системный рефактор

- Abbreviation-first writing is the zone's defining habit: 140 unexpanded abbreviations across only 6.0k words of article prose (24.5 per 1k). The pattern is structural, not accidental — abbreviations are introduced in section HEADINGS ('## CIA Triad', '## Алгоритмы подписи — HS256 vs RS256', '## A10: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)'), where there is no room for a gloss, and then used freely in the body. 07-owasp-top-10.md and 08-security-interview-questions.md are the worst (13 and 21 flags in 295 and 670 words) because they are index/revision files that name every concept and explain none. Fix pattern: put the expansion in the first body sentence under each heading, not in the heading.
- Sections systematically skip the lead sentence and open straight into a fenced block. 02 ('## Фундаментальное различие'), 03 ('## Access Token + Refresh Token'), 06 ('## Hashing vs Encryption'), 01 ('## HTTPS и TLS') open with a ```txt diagram; 07's A05, A06, A07 and A09 open with ```typescript. The reader gets the comparison table before being told what is being compared. This is why C averages 3.4 in a zone whose sentences (B 3.85) and examples (E 3.9) are otherwise strong: the language is clear, but the pyramid is inverted at section level.
- The RU quiz bank is machine-translated where the RU question bank is hand-written, and they disagree on core terminology: 'prepared statements' is 'подготовленные выражения' in questions/security.json but 'подготовленные утверждения' in quiz/security.json; 'token' is 'токен' in half the quiz items and 'маркер' in the other half; 'output encoding and input validation' became 'кодирование выхода и валидацию входа'; 'defense in depth' became 'защиту в глубину'. Item 19 has a grammar error ('для кража кода авторизации'). The quiz is the only file in the zone scoring G=2.

**Прочее:** Correctness findings (report even though not readability): (1) HARD CONTRADICTION — topics/security/{ru,en}/07-owasp-top-10.md returns 403 on a failed ownership check with the comment '// не 404 — утечка info' / '// not 404 — info leak', while questions/security.json security-q-12 names exactly that a 'Common pitfall' and returns 404 with '// 404, not 403 — don't confirm existence'. The article's comment is also backwards on its own terms: 403 is the leaking response. (2) quiz item 25's correct answer says the cookie flags 'block XSS via JS', and item 13's explanation says 'HttpOnly prevents XSS from stealing the session token' — 04-xss-csrf-cors.md lists this belief under 'Типичные ошибки на интервью' and security-q-6 contradicts it directly. (3) quiz items 23/17/14 state flatly that 'CSP prevents XSS'; the article calls CSP 'последний рубеж обороны' and security-q-10 calls it 'a second layer of defense' — the quiz teaches CSP as a primary control. (4) quiz-18's explanation calls SameSite cookies an 'anti-CSRF token' ('like SameSite cookies or synchronizer tokens') — a category error. (5) quiz-24 claims the Authorization Code flow keeps the access token on the backend 'where it's safely stored and used server-to-server'; that describes a BFF, not plain Authorization Code, and security-q-9 (PKCE for public clients) implies the opposite for SPAs. Token storage, password hashing and CORS are CONSISTENT across all three surfaces — no localStorage-for-tokens defect of the browser-runtime kind exists here; every source says memory or HttpOnly cookie. Quiz counts as requested: correctIndex distribution 0→25, 1→0, 2→0, 3→0; correct option is the longest option in 24/25 items (EN) and 23/25 (RU); by word count 24/25 (EN), 22/25 (RU). Also: 21 of 25 quiz items are near-duplicates of five questions (XSS stored-vs-reflected ×4, JWT structure ×5, OAuth code flow ×5, CSP ×4, cookie flags ×3), leaving SQL injection, secrets, SSRF, IDOR, rate limiting and supply chain almost untested. Minor code defect: 05-sql-injection-and-input-validation.md uses path.extname(fileType.ext) — fileType.ext is 'jpg', not a filename, so path.extname returns '' and the saved file gets no extension.

### solid-grasp (вопросы+quiz) — системный рефактор

- The quiz is answerable without reading it. correctIndex is 0 in 20/24 and never 2 or 3 (guessing A scores 83%), and the correct option is the longest of the four in 15/24 en / 17/24 ru because only the correct option carries a trailing '— because ...' clause. This is the third quiz bank in a row with exactly this shape (quiz/oop-patterns: 18/25 at index 0, 22/25 longest-correct), so it is a generator default, not a per-file accident: fix it once in the generation template, not item by item.
- The quiz was assembled from per-language generation batches that were never read end to end. The tells cluster: 8/24 items (quiz-11/12/14/15 `java`, quiz-22/23/24/25 `typescript`) have the language tag with no ``` fence in BOTH locales, so the code renders as raw prose; four of them are Java on a Node/React site; id `solid-grasp-quiz-21` is missing from a 1-25 range; quiz-12's stem still opens 'Consider a payment processing system' above a Rectangle/Shape example; quiz-25's distractor still says 'errors that Rectangle doesn't'. Item content duplicates in blocks too — 4 near-identical SRP items (1, 6, 11, 16), 4 DIP-inject-an-interface items (9, 14, 18, 24), 3 ISP forced-stub items (13, 19, 25), and the same Square/Rectangle LSP question twice (12 in Java, 23 in TypeScript).
- The quiz contradicts the site's own theory and itself on GRASP taxonomy. quiz-20 asserts Mediator is a GRASP pattern (the article 02-grasp-patterns.md lists seven, Mediator is not among them; 05-behavioral-patterns.md documents it as GoF) and marks the real GRASP answer 'Low Coupling' wrong; quiz-5 marks non-GRASP Factory correct in a GRASP question with Creator wrong; quiz-8 then says 'Factory (Creator)' are the same thing. Meanwhile the QUESTION bank gets all of this right and goes further than the article (it covers Indirection and Protected Variations, which 02-grasp-patterns.md does not). The two files in one zone teach different facts.
- The question bank is the opposite problem: excellent, internally consistent, senior-level content trapped in over-long single sentences. 57.8% of en sentences exceed 25 words vs 39% ru, so the English is measurably harder than the Russian for the same content. The structural habit is one long sentence carrying a definition plus a parenthetical list plus a contrast clause, all joined by an em-dash — the fix is mechanical (split at the em-dash and the colon) and does not touch a single technical claim.
- The Russian question bank leaves the load-bearing vocabulary in English. «Trade-off» is untranslated in all 25 entries, plus `actor'у/actor'ам/actor'а/actor'ов` (English noun + Russian case ending via apostrophe, q-1/q-8/q-21), `failure mode` (q-7, q-13), «коллабораторами» (q-6/q-19/q-25) and «заботы» as a calque of "concerns" (7×). q-21 additionally contains an ungrammatical machine-translation seam («превращает корень агрегата в разбитые на валидатор...»).

**Прочее:** Overlap with questions/oop-patterns.json is near zero, not high: 0 of its 34 entries mention SOLID, GRASP, or any of the five principles by name — it is pure GoF (Singleton, Builder, Decorator, Observer, Command, Bridge, Facade, Proxy, Flyweight, State, Mediator, Null Object...). Only 2 of solid-grasp's 25 overlap: q-9 Factory Method (vs oop-patterns q-2/q-11) and q-10 Adapter (vs q-18). Verdict: keep them as two banks. The real problem is the opposite of duplication — solid-grasp's 25 excellent questions are the ONLY SOLID/GRASP practice on the site, and the articles that explain the theory (topics/oop-patterns/*/01-solid-principles.md, 02-grasp-patterns.md, rated 4-5 by the oop-patterns audit) sit behind a different page the reader never visits. Suggest surfacing those two articles from the solid-grasp page; if that is not possible, the acronym expansions in the quiz stop being optional. Also worth noting: the solid-grasp question bank covers Indirection and Protected Variations, which 02-grasp-patterns.md does not — so the article should gain those two sections rather than the bank losing them.

### state-management (статьи) — точечные правки

- An abbreviation is introduced inside a section heading and expanded late or never. RTK stands in the H2 of article 03 and is used 15 times without ever being spelled out as Redux Toolkit; HOC stands in the H2 of article 01; SSR, RSC, SWR, DI, SPA and OOP all first appear inside comparison tables and bullet lists. The heading is what the reader sees first in a phone table of contents, so it is the worst possible place to put a cold acronym.
- The question bank (06) compresses a numbered list of 3-4 independent facts into a single sentence: 'It differs from a plain getter in three ways: (1)... (2)... (3)...' (80 words EN / 59 RU), the same shape in Q6, Q14, Q15, Q25. The list structure already exists in the text — only the sentence boundaries are missing. This is the only rubric-B problem in the zone, but it is concentrated and it is in the file people revise from.
- Articles 01, 02 and 04 model 'fetch API data into the store' (fetchUser, fetchProducts, login) as the ordinary shape of an async action, with loading/error flags and no caching. The topic's own correction — server state belongs to React Query / SWR / RTK Query — arrives only in articles 05 and 06, and only article 03 mentions it in place (RTK Query). Because the topic has no server-state chapter at all, a reader who reads just the MobX or Zustand article leaves having learned the pattern the topic later calls 'reinventing the wheel'. One caveat sentence at the end of each async section fixes this without touching the examples.
- RU files keep English formatting labels and jargon words untranslated inside Russian prose ('**Store configuration:**', '**TypeScript experience:**', '## Async в Zustand — без ceremony', 'воспроизведения bagов'), and RU 05 has drifted from EN: it still contains a dead `get subtotal()` getter that the EN file deleted. Worth a diff pass RU↔EN across the zone, not just a language pass.

**Прочее:** Articles 01-05 are the strongest prose in the zone: leads answer first, every new idea gets a code example immediately, and the RU is genuinely readable (B and C average 3.4 / 4.1). The damage is concentrated in three places — cold acronyms, the question bank's crammed enumerations, and the two RU/EN drift bugs in 05. EN is measurably harder than RU in 06 (17 long sentences vs 9; the same answer is 80 words in EN and 59 in RU), which is the usual ~19% expansion pushing borderline RU sentences over the EN limit. I treated 'UI' as a false positive from the flag script (same tier as API/HTML for this reader) but kept DOM and JSX, which are not.

### strapi (статьи) — системный рефактор

- The structural habit that defines this zone: **heading, then straight into a code block, with no sentence in between.** 24 of the 33 body sections across the seven articles do this. Measured, every file is 52-75% code by word count (ru/05: 629 of 848 words; ru/06: 666 of 890; en/02: 571 of 797). The consequence is that every concept in the topic is introduced by name inside a code comment or an ASCII table rather than defined in prose — Policy, Middleware, API Token, Dynamic Zone, Component, Bootstrap, Register, Cron Job, EventHub, Query Engine, sanitizeOutput. The reader is asked to infer the idea from a 50-line TypeScript listing on a phone. Nothing here needs cutting; each of those sections needs a 3-5 sentence lead added above the existing code.
- **The teaching has migrated to the bottom of the file.** The «Типичные ошибки на интервью» / «Common interview mistakes» bullet list carries 64-96% of all non-code words in every article 01-06 (ru/05: 211 of 219 prose words = 96%; en/03: 228 of 252 = 90%; en/05: 240 of 250 = 96%).
